nota: L'alternanza β/δ (dorico ὀδελός) è stata indicata come tratto pre-greco. Da verificare.
Paretimologia diffusa: le statue «senza cera», cioè non ritoccate. Respinta dagli etimologisti.
Forse dalla sillaba infantile *mā- con il suffisso dei nomi di parentela *-tēr. Da verificare.
From Late Latin abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”).
Derived from Latin decadem, accusative of decas. By surface analysis, deca- + -ade.
Inherited from Latin sēmen, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.
Combining form of Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”).
Inherited from Late Latin sabbatum. Compare English Sabbath.
Metathesis from Latin āera, Greek-type accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). See also aere.
From Arabic اَلْجَزَائِر (al-jazāʔir, “the islands”), plural of جَزِيرَة (jazīra, “island”), referring to the several small islands that once existed in the Bay of Algiers.
Learned borrowing from Latin monētārius (“of or belonging to the mint”).
Borrowed from Latin acācia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía, “shittah tree”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point”). Doublet of gaggia.
From the Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognate with Sicilian cani.
Borrowed from English koala, from Dharug gula or gulawany.
From Late Latin fīnālis, from Latin fīnis (“end; boundary, limit”), whence fine. By surface analysis, fine (“end; limit; goal”) + -ale.
Borrowed from Latin lupus. Doublet of lovo and the inherited lupo.
Learned borrowing from Latin facem (“torch, firebrand”).
Inherited from Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).
Inherited from Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.
Borrowed from French menu. Doublet of minuto.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin magnesia.
From Latin colōrem, from Old Latin colos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).
Borrowed from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”).
From Latin ēta, from Ancient Greek ἦτα (êta), later form of ἧτα (hêta), from Phoenician 𐤇 (ḥ /⁠ḥēt⁠/), whence also heth.
Borrowed from English premier, itself a borrowing from French premier, ultimately from Classical Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primaio, primiero, and primario.
Learned borrowing from Latin ārea. Doublet of aia (“threshing floor”).
From New Latin neon, from Ancient Greek νέον (néon), neuter form of νέος (néos, “new”).
From Latin inde (“thence, from that place; from that person, of them”). Compare French en (adverb, pronoun).
Unadapted borrowing from French croissant, present participle of verb croître (“to grow”). Doublet of crescente.
Borrowed from English slogan, from Scottish Gaelic sluagh-ghairm (“battle cry”).
From Latin vōs, from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs. Cognates with the same usage are the French vous and the Russian вы (vy).
From Medieval Latin algebra, from Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr, “reunion, resetting of broken parts”).
From Latin testa. The semantic development is earthen pot → skull → head.
Borrowed from English cross. The sense "motocross" is a pseudo-anglicism, derived from English motocross.

From Latin Brundisium, from Ancient Greek Βρεντέσιον (Brentésion), said to be from the Messapic word for the head of a male deer, possibly based on the shape of the port. Compare Proto-Albanian *brina (Albanian bri) and *drani (Albanian dre).
From Latin Placentia, from placentia, from placēns (“pleasing, welcoming”).
From Latin Tarentum, from Ancient Greek Τάρᾱς (Tárās), probably from Illyrian *darandos (“oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”), which also yields Albanian dru (“wood, tree”).
Inherited from Latin Tridentum (literally “three teeth”), named for the three hills that surround the city.
From Latin Tarvisium, Tarvisum, from the name of the Celtic tribe, Taurusci.
Inherited from Latin candēla, derived from candeō (“to shine, glow”).
From Latin sīc. In the “yes” sense, from sīc (est).
Unadapted borrowing from English humour. Doublet of umore.
From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).
Borrowed from Portuguese cobra, from Old Galician-Portuguese coobra, from Latin colubra, feminine of coluber (“snake, serpent”).
From Latin alopecia, from Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκία (alōpekía).
From Latin fōrmōsus (“beautiful, well-formed”) (compare Portuguese formoso, Spanish hermoso, Galician fermoso, Romanian frumos).
Borrowed from French est, from Old English ēast.
Inherited from Latin antenna, the scientific senses were borrowed later.
Borrowed from Latin focus, whence also Italian fuoco (an inherited doublet).
Probably borrowed from Latin bēstia, but some sources consider it inherited. Cognate to biscia, which is definitely inherited.
From the form vìnchio, from Late Latin vinclum, from Latin vinculum. Compare the borrowed doublet vincolo.
Learned borrowing from Latin placēbō (“I will please”), the first-person singular future active indicative of placeō (“to please”).
From Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
From Latin pugna, from pugnō (“to fight, oppose”), from pugnus (“fist”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
Borrowed from Latin fuga. Compare the inherited doublet foga.
Learned borrowing from Latin clādēs (“breaking; destruction”)
Unadapted borrowing from English ticket. Doublet of etichetta.
Inherited from Latin chorda (“cord”), from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”).

From Luna, from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).
From (combining form of) Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).
Inherited from Old Italian laco, from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).
From Latin lavāre (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”).
Borrowed from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis.
From Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Cognate with Sicilian lucali.
From Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”).
From Latin lacertula, diminutive of lacerta (“lizard”). Doublet of alligatore. Compare Galician, Spanish, and Portuguese lagarto (“lizard”).
Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina. Doublet of pania.
From earlier lengua, from Latin lingua.
Learned borrowing from Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís, “missile, arrow, javelin”).
From Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face”).
Borrowed from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”). By surface analysis, biblio- + -teca.
Inherited from Latin nivem, from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs. Compare Portuguese neve, Spanish nieve.
From Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).

From older notare, from Vulgar Latin *notāre, from Latin natāre. Compare Corsican nutà, Romanian înota. The original Italian notare had no diphthong in the infinitive, but it did have conjugations such as nuota (“swims”), reflecting the regular diphthongization of Latin /ŏ/ in a stressed open syllable. Eventually the diphthong spread to all forms of the verb, including the infinitive. Doublet of natare.

Inherited from Late Latin auca, syncope of *avica, from Classical Latin avis (“bird”). Compare Catalan, Spanish, Venetan, and Sicilian oca, French oie, Occitan auca, Romansh auca, ocha, Friulian ocje, Dalmatian jauca.
From Latin rārus. Doublet of rado.
Borrowed from Latin raucus. Compare roco, an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).
From Old French fieu (“fief”), from Frankish *fehu, from Proto-Germanic *fehu, from Proto-Indo-European *péḱu (“livestock”).
Borrowed from English sketch from Dutch schets, from Italian schizzo, from Latin schedium, from Ancient Greek σχέδιος (skhédios, “made suddenly, off-hand”).
Latinization of older matera, from Latin māteria.
Clipping of allelomorfo, compare English allele.
From Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).
Borrowed from French hôtel, from Middle French hostel (“hostel”, “inn”), from Old French ostel (“shelter”), from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospedale and ospitale.
From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
Borrowed from Old French saie, from Latin sagum.
Unadapted borrowing from French pendant. Doublet of pendente.
From Latin vectōrem. Cognate with Piedmontese vetur.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”).
Inherited from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, paper”).
Borrowed from Arabic قِيثَارَة (qīṯāra), from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of cetra, inherited from Latin.
Inherited from Latin clāvus with /aw/ > /ɔ/ and then insertion of an epenthetic /d/ (possibly chosen by analogy with chiudere).
Pseudo-anglicism, derived from a clipping of English jolly joker, an older name for the joker card in a deck of cards.
Borrowed from French oxygène. By surface analysis, ossi- (“oxy-”) + -geno (“-gen”).
From Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
Borrowed from English millibar. By surface analysis, milli- + bar.
From Turkish kebap, from Arabic كَبَاب (kabāb, “fried meat”).
From Latin nānus, from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos).
Inherited from Latin famem (“hunger”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, French faim, Portuguese fome and Romanian foame, Sicilian fami.
Borrowed from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís. Doublet of s-.
Inherited from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse”, “treasure”). Doublet of Tesauro (“a male given name”).
From Ancient Greek ἐπι- (epi-), from ἐπί (epí, “on top of”).
Coined based on Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”).
Inherited from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment”).
Derived from Old Italian patre, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *passātus, perfect passive participle of *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).
Inherited from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).
Borrowed from Latin pavīmentum. Doublet of Old Italian palmiento, inherited.
Borrowed from Latin prīncipium, derived from prīncipis, princĭpis, genitive singular of prīnceps (“first”) (compare principe (“prince”) from the meaning "chief").
From Latin arcus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo- (“bow, arrow”).
From Latin abūsīvus, equivalent to abuso + -ivo.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin bonus, either through English or influenced by English. Compare the inherited doublet buono (“good”).
Borrowed from French patron. Doublet of padrone.
Borrowed from Latin super. Cf. sopra.
From Latin altus (“high”), from Proto-Italic *altos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós, derived from the root *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”). Cognate with English old and Welsh allt.
Borrowed from Latin chaos from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos).

Borrowed from Old Occitan aize, from Vulgar Latin *adjace(m), from Latin adjacēns, present participle of adjaceō (compare Medieval Latin in aiace). Cognate with Old French aise, eise, French aise and aisance; compare also Catalan eina. Doublet of adiacente.
Borrowed from Latin alacrem (“lively, brisk; happy”). Doublet of allegro.
Borrowed from Latin valē (“be well, goodbye”).
Borrowed from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta (“cake”), from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta, “flat”).
From Late Latin cucutia (via metathesis and apheresis), from Latin cucurbita (“gourd”). Doublet of cocuzza and cucurbita.
Inherited from Late Latin bassus, possibly of Ancient Greek origin.
Borrowed from Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρᾱτής (peirātḗs), derived from πειράω (peiráō, “to try, attempt”).

From Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). By surface analysis, gelo (“frost, cold”) + -ato (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.” Akin to Russian моро́женое (moróženoje).
Inherited from Latin pilōsus. By surface analysis, pelo (“fur, hair”) + -oso (“-ous”).
Inherited from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).

From a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *clociola, diminutive of *clocea, from metathesis of Latin cochlea (“snail”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías), cognate with κόχλος (kókhlos, “shellfish”). Compare with Sardinian còciola and Sicilian còzzula.
Unadapted borrowing from English clan. Ultimately a doublet of pianta.
Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).
From a variant of Late Latin modulus.
Inherited from Latin mulier (nominative). The alternative forms reflect the Latin accusative mulierem.
From Latin intrā, with influence from Latin inter.
Inherited from Latin con-, from cum (“with”).
Inherited from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).
Inherited from Latin gravis. Doublet of greve.
From Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.
Borrowed from Latin discus. Doublet of desco, which was inherited.
Inherited from Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).
Inherited from Latin costa. Cognate with French côte, Romanian coastă, and Spanish cuesta.
From Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos.
Probably borrowed from Latin ferreus. By surface analysis, ferro (“iron”) + -eo.
Learned borrowing from Latin cicatrīcem, cicatricem.
Borrowed from English mascara, from Italian (archaic) mascara. Doublet of maschera.
From Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-. Compare Spanish mosca.
From Late Latin vanga, of Germanic origin; compare Old Norse vangsni (“ploughshare”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ). Compare French acmé.
Borrowed from Latin phantasma, or Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma).
Inherited from Latin lignum. Cognates include Spanish leño, Romanian lemn.
From tri- + nitro- + toluene, superseded the previous trinitrotoluolo. Compare tritolo.
Borrowed from Latin aurōra, from an ā-stem extension of Proto-Italic *auzōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsōs.
Inherited from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).
From Late Latin sanguem, alteration of Classical Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare French sang, Romanian sânge.
Borrowed from Old French mangier, from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manicare, and manucare.
Inherited from Latin illōrum, genitive plural of ille, illud (“that”).

Inherited from Latin illaei. The formal address Lei appears in the 16th century in connection with Signoria (“Lordship”), Eccellenza (“Excellency”), Santità (“Holiness”) and Magnificenza, alongside Voi.

From Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos. In the singular, Latin tuum underwent *ʊu > *ou > *ɔu dissimilation, cf. Sardinian tou, and also Latin ōvum > Italian òvo, Spanish huevo, ultimately producing [ˈtwɔu], and a plural [ˈtwɔi]. Italian then underwent its regular *wɔV > *uV sound change, cf. *bwɔe > bue, *mjɛu > mio, producing ultimately [ˈtu.o]. This latter sound change is blocked by a following [i], which explains the plural form tuoi, cf. *mjɛi > miei.

From earlier spata, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē), from Proto-Indo-European *sph₂dʰh₁éh₂, derived from *(s)peh₂- (“to draw”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to put”) + *-eh₂ (feminine noun ending). Doublet of spata.
From Latin studeō, or through studio, from Latin studium. By surface analysis, studio + -are. Compare Spanish estudiar.
Inherited from Latin prandium, whence also Dalmatian prinz and Romanian prânz. Ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin.
Borrowed from Late Latin clīma, from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, incline”).
From Late Latin lamentōsus. By surface analysis, lamento + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin virtuōsus. By surface analysis, virtù + -oso.
Unadapted borrowing from English blitz, shortened from English blitzkrieg, from German Blitzkrieg.
From Francia + -ese. Borrowed from Old French franceis.
Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin pigrum. See also peritarsi, which was inherited from a derivative verb pīgritārī.
From Latin salvus. Cognate to French sauf.
Inherited from Latin hāmus. Compare Spanish hamo, French hameçon.
From New Latin Agave, from Ancient Greek Ἀγαυή (Agauḗ), name of one of the daughters of Cadmus, from ἀγαυός (agauós, “noble, illustrious”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ, “the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω (aortéō), lengthened form of ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”).
From Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “garland, wreath”). Compare also cruna, probably from a derivative of the same Latin word.
Borrowed from Venetan doxe, from Latin ducem (“leader; commander; ruler”). Doublet of duce and duca.
From Latin fovea. Doublet of foiba.
Inherited from Latin glaber (“smooth; hairless”), through an archaic meaning of "uncultivated, barren land".
From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian hbj.
Borrowed from Latin magma, from Ancient Greek μάγμα (mágma).
Unadapted borrowing from French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).
From Latin penna and pinna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).
Borrowed from Latin schema, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).
From Latin servus, from Proto-Indo-European *ser-wo- (“guardian”), or perhaps of Etruscan origin.

Unadapted borrowing from French chef (“head; chief”), from Middle French chief, from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of capo.
From Latin chimaera, from Ancient Greek Χίμαιρα (Khímaira).
Inherited from Latin fascia. Compare Spanish haza, Portuguese faixa, Romanian fașă.
From French vedette, from Italian vedetta.
Borrowed from Latin verbēna. Compare the doublet vermena.
From Latin colōnia (“colony”), from colōnus (“farmer; colonist”), from colō (“till, cultivate, worship”).
From Portuguese macaco, possibly from a Bantu language.
Unadapted borrowing from German Quantum, from Latin quantum. Doublet of quanto, which was also re-borrowed with the same meaning as quantum. First attested before 1930.
Unadapted borrowing from English intelligence. Doublet of intelligenza and intellighenzia.
From Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).
From Latin capra, from its masculine version caper, from Proto-Italic *kapros, from Proto-Indo-European *kápros.
From Latin unda, from nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aer-.
Inherited from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios).
From Latin pauperem. Given that the expect native reflex would have been *popere, this form was likely among the early borrowings into Italian from Gallo-Italic.
Borrowed from Latin pūblicus. Doublet of piuvico, which is inherited.
Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge, Old French corage.
Borrowed from English shampoo, from Hindi चाँपो (cā̃po, “knead!”), from the Sanskrit root चपयति (capayati, “to pound, to knead”).
From Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum, from the verb speciō. Compare specolo, a borrowed doublet.
Borrowed from Latin speciēs. Doublet of spezie.

From Medieval Latin or Late Latin dentālis, derived from Latin dēns (“tooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts. By surface analysis, dent(e) (“tooth”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).
From Latin amethystus, from Ancient Greek ἀμέθυστος (améthustos, “remedy against inebriation”), from ἀ- (a-) (privative prefix) + μεθύειν (methúein, “to become inebriated”).
From Latin Syria, from Ancient Greek Συρία (Suría).
From Vulgar Latin *ungla, syncopated form of Latin ungula, from unguis.
Inherited from Latin spissus. Compare Spanish espeso, Portuguese espesso, French épais.

From Early Medieval Latin theodiscus, from a Germanic language, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of the people, popular, vernacular”), from *þeudō (“people”) + *-iskaz (“-ish, -ic, -al”). The Old English form is þēodisċ, the Old High German one diutisc (attested ca. 1090 in the Annolied). Compare also Friulian todesc, archaic or regional French thiois, Sicilian tudiscu.
Inherited from Latin radius. Doublet of razzo, radio, and rai, which were respectively inherited from Latin, borrowed from Latin, and borrowed from Occitan.
From Latin fūrtum, derived from fūr (“thief”).
Borrowed from Old French romanz, which stems from the Latin expression romanice loqui (“to speak in the Roman way”). Cognate with English romance (noun).
From Latin imperātōrem. Documented since the twelfth century. Synchronically derivable from imperare + -tore.
From earlier *strata, from Late Latin strāta (“paved road”), from Latin [via] strāta, feminine of strātus, perfect passive participle of sternō.
From Old Italian istoria, borrowed from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, “learning through research”).
From Ancient Greek ἀξιωματικός (axiōmatikós), in turn from ἀξίωμα (axíōma).
From giocare + -tore. Compare French joueur, Piedmontese giugador and giugheur, Portuguese jogador, Romanian jucător, Spanish jugador.
From Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).

From Spagna (“Spain”) + -olo (“derivative suffix”), possibly also from Old Occitan espaignol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispāniolus, from Latin Hispānus. Compare French espagnol, Portuguese espanhol, Spanish español. Doublet of épagneul.
Learned borrowing from Latin ratiō (“reason, explanation”).
Internationalism. Ultimately an unadapted borrowing from Latin locus (“place, spot”). Doublet of luogo.
Borrowed from Latin cavea. Doublet of gaggia and gabbia.
From Latin cavea. Doublet of cavea, a later borrowing. Cognates include Catalan gàbia, English cage, Sicilian jaggia
Uncertain if inherited or borrowed from Latin vapōrem.
From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of Augusto.
From Late Latin sapphīrus, from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros, “lapis lazuli”).
From Ancient Greek ζύγωμα (zúgōma), from ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm (“yoke”).
Borrowed from Spanish zamarra, chamarra, possibly from Arabic سَمُّور (sammūr), from Persian سمور (samur).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin zizania, from Ancient Greek ζιζάνια (zizánia), plural of ζιζάνιον (zizánion).
Inherited from Latin sulphur, sulfur. For the initial z- compare also zoccolo. Cognate with Sicilian sùrfuru and Venetan solfaro.
Borrowed from Latin invidia (“envy”). Doublet of the obsolete inveggia, itself probably taken from Old Occitan.
From in- + grasso + -are Compare French engraisser, Dalmatian engrassur, Spanish engrasar, Romanian îngrășa.
Borrowed from Old Occitan semblar, from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). More or less a doublet of somigliare.

From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin cloppus, perhaps ultimately imitative of a limping person. The Italian was possibly altered by influence from zanca. Compare Romanian șchiop, cf. also Catalan and Occitan esclop, Old French clop and Sicilian zoppu.
Probably a borrowing from (Medieval) Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ).
From Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathēdrālis, from Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).
Learned borrowing from Latin abortīre, from abortus.
Borrowed from French agir, itself borrowed from Latin agere.
Inherited from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”). Doublet of city.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin quōrum, genitive plural form of quī (“who, which”).
From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum (deictic) + iste (“that”), the former surviving also as Italian ecco and the latter as esto.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātiōnem.
Inherited from Latin habitūdinem. By surface analysis, abito + -itudine.
Borrowed from English bomber. The sense "bomber jacket" is a pseudo-anglicism.
From Medieval Latin affictāre, itself from fictus.
From Ancient Greek πρωτο- (prōto-), combining form of πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”), superlative of πρό (pró, “before”).
From Portuguese pagode, which is via Malayalam പകോതി (pakōti) from Sanskrit भगवती (Bhagavatī, name of a goddess) or भागवत (Bhāgavata, “follower of Bhagavatī”).

Uncertain. Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, itself either from Latin datum (“thrown, given”), or from Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese dado, Catalan dau, French dé (whence English die).
Inherited from Latin damnum, from Proto-Italic *dapnom, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnóm (“expense, investment”), derived from *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice”).
From Latin futūrus (future participle of esse).
Borrowed from English audience, from Latin audientia, derived from audiēns, present active participle of audiō (“to hear, listen to”).
Unadapted borrowing from English forum, borrowed from Latin forum. Doublet of foro.
Inherited from Latin radius. Doublet of raggio, radio, and rai, which were respectively inherited from Latin, borrowed from Latin, and borrowed from Occitan.
From decadere + -enza, based on the example of French décadence. Cf. also Late Latin decadentia.
Borrowed from Late Latin decimālis, from Latin decimus.
Inherited from Latin grandem, of unclear origin.
Derived from Latin brūtus. Doublet of bruto.
From older basciare, inherited from Latin bāsiāre (“to kiss”).
From Vulgar Latin *baneāre, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare French baigner, Sicilian vagnari, Spanish bañar.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin balcōnem. Compare Old Italian balco (“scaffold”).
From Late Latin barca, derived from Latin baris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris), itself probably from Egyptian bꜣjr (“transport ship”).

By surface analysis, *bara + -ella, of Germanic origin, borrowed from Lombardic *bāra (“stretcher, bier”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *bāru, from Proto-Germanic *bērō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry, bear”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Beere (“stretcher, bier”), Dutch baar (“bier”), German Bahre (“bier, stretcher”) and Sicilian vara. Not related to bara.
Borrowed from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”). Doublet of the inherited ora.
From Medieval Latin aqueus. By surface analysis, acqu(a) (“water”) + -eo (“-ous”).
From Latin quaternus (“fourfold”), from quater (“four times”), from quattuor (“four”).
From Latin quadrātus, from quadrō (“to make square”), from quattuor (“four”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
Borrowed from Latin sarcoma, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + -ωμα (-ōma, “process”) or from Ancient Greek σαρκόω (sarkóō), itself from σάρξ (sárx).
Borrowed from Latin dogma, from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “belief”).
From Latin carcĭnōma (“a cancerous ulcer”), from Ancient Greek καρκίνωμα (karkínōma).
Borrowed from French cinéma, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “movement”).
From Latin asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
From Latin avus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwh₂os. Compare Portuguese avô (“grandfather”) and avó (“grandmother”).
Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.
From Latin audīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”).
Borrowed from Latin bulbus, from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).
From Latin paenīnsula (“peninsula”), from paene (“almost”) + īnsula (“island”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula. Doublet of macula, a borrowing.
From a Latin nūbila, noun use of the feminine of nūbilus (“cloudy”), from nūbēs. Cognate with Sicilian nuvula. Compare Catalan núvol.
Borrowed from Latin perīculum. Doublet of the archaic periglio.
From Latin cervus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂wós, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“horn”).
Learned borrowing from Latin super-. Doublet of sopra- and sovra-.
Borrowed from Latin plēbem. Compare the inherited doublet pieve.
From older virtute, from Latin virtūtem. This form may reflect some semi-learned influence; cf. the variant vertù.
Inherited from Old Italian pietade, pietate, from Latin pietātem (“piety”, “pity”). By surface analysis, pio (“pious”) + -età (“-ity”).
Borrowed from Latin pallidus, derived from palleō (“to be pale”).
Inherited from Latin flātus. Doublet of flato.
Borrowed from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”).
From gocciare or from a Vulgar Latin *guttia or *guttea; ultimately from Latin gutta.
Borrowed from Latin machina (“engine, device, mill”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Compare the inherited doublet macina (“grindstone”).
From Ancient Greek νεκροφόρος (nekrophóros). By surface analysis, necro- (“necro-”, “death”) + -foro (“-phore”, “bearer”, “carrier”).
From Latin pāpiliōnem (“military tent”). Compare French pavillon. Doublet of papiglione.
From contado (“countryside”) + -ino (“diminutive suffix”). Compare Sicilian cuntatinu.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek αἱμο- (haimo-), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).
Borrowed from Latin victōria, from vincere.
From earlier equale, from Latin aequālis, derived from aequus (“equal, even”).

Inherited from Latin quasi. The final -i seems to hint towards the word being borrowed or semi-learned, but it's not uncommon for Italian to shift final -e to -i in invariable words (cf. avanti, dieci, tardi, etc.).
Back-formation as a masculine noun from the plural paia, from Latin paria (“even, equal”, neuter plural of pār). Cognate with Sicilian paru.

Borrowed from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward”), from prefix προ- (pro-, “in front of”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw, to cast, to hurl”).
From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek διάστημα (diástēma).
Inherited from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rēgālia, “gratuity” sense influenced by regalare.
Borrowed from Old French fleche, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, of Frankish origin.
Borrowed from Latin Scōtia, after the population of Scōtī, a term of possible Celtic origin.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin irrēgulāris.
Inherited from Latin cal(i)dus. Doublet of calido, which was borrowed.
From Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”).
From Latin nocturnus, from noctū (“by night”), from nox (“night”), whence also Italian notte, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
From Latin Marius. By folk etymology seen as a masculine form of Maria.
From Old Italian camarlingo, inherited from Medieval Latin camarlingus. Doublet of ciambellano. Cognates include Old High German chamarling and French chambellan.
Borrowed from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).
From Late Latin missa, from Latin missum.
From Late Latin martellus, diminutive of martulus, variant of Latin marculus, diminutive of marcus, or from malleus (“hammer”). Compare Portguese martelo and Catalan martell.
From Latin pactum from pacisci (“to make an accordance”).
From Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía).
Inherited from Latin pōmum (“fruit”), from pōmus, from Proto-Italic *poomos, probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”), from *h₂epo (“off”) + *h₁em- (“take”).
From Latin mentum, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to project”).
Inherited from Latin stilus. Doublet of stilo and stile, which were borrowed from Latin and French respectively.

From Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom. See also the obsolete variant form ariento, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *aregentum; cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish arento, Spanish arienzo.
From corno (“horn”, from Latin cornū) + -etto (diminutive suffix).
From Late Latin zeugma, from Ancient Greek ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “bond; yoking”).
From a reduction of the prefix in discendere, from Latin dēscendere.
From Latin scheda (“piece of paper”), from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”). Doublet of sceda.
Derived from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía).
Borrowed from Old French boiste, whence French boîte (“box”). Derived from Medieval Latin buxida, inflected form derived from Latin buxētum (“boxwood plantation”), from Latin buxus (“boxwood”).
Inherited from Latin semper; compare Catalan and Portuguese sempre, Spanish siempre.
Borrowed from Latin regiōnem, case form of regiō (literally “direction, line”), derived from regō (“to rule, govern”). Compare rione, an inherited doublet.

From Latin faenum (“hay”), which derives from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-. Another proposed etymology is a Vulgar Latin *flēnum, from a blending of flōs (“flower”) and faenum. Cognate with Sicilian frenu.
Inherited from Latin nūlla, feminine singular and neuter plural (collective) of nūllus.
Borrowed from French style, itself borrowed from Latin stilus. Doublet of stelo and stilo, which Italian inherited and borrowed from Latin respectively.
From Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”), + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”), corresponding to ana- + -archia.
Unadapted borrowing from English compost. Doublet of composto.
Borrowed from Latin limbus. Doublet of lembo, inherited.
Borrowed from Latin servitium, from servus (“slave”). Compare Portuguese serviço, French service, Norman sèrvice, Sicilian sirbizzu, Spanish servicio.
Derived from Latin dormītōrium, possibly a borrowing.
From Medieval Latin, Late Latin laudum, from Latin laudō.
Derived from Latin curvus (“bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn; to bend”).
From Latin campus (“wild field”). Compare English camp.
Borrowed from Latin tranquillus (“quiet, calm, still, tranquil”), from Proto-Italic *trānskʷīlos.
Borrowed from English ranch. Cognate with English rank; doublet of rancio.
Borrowed from Latin dēlīctum, from dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”); probably a semi-learned borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin uterīnus (“uterine”).
Borrowed from Latin urbānus (“of or belonging to a city”), derived from urbs (“city”). By surface analysis, urbe (“city”) + -ano (pertaining to).
Borrowed from Latin quantitātem, from quantus.
Borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium. Doublet of gaudio. Cognate with Sicilian gioja.
Borrowed from English picnic, from French pique-nique.
Borrowed from French responsable, assimilated to the native suffix -abile. Cognate with Piedmontese responsàbil.
Borrowed from Classical Latin ūniversitātem (“the whole” → (Late Latin) “(whole) group; company; corporation” → (Medieval Latin) “university”).
From New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”).
From New Latin chlorum, from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χρῶμᾰ (khrômă).
From New Latin cōbaltum, derived from German Kobalt, derived from Kobolet, alteration of Kobold (“elf, goblin”).
Borrowed from New Latin selēnium, from Ancient Greek Σελήνη (Selḗnē, “moon”).
From earlier platina, from Spanish platina, diminutive of plata (“silver”).
Learned borrowing from Latin odium (“hate”), whence also uggia, inherited through Vulgar Latin.
Inherited from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.
Borrowed from Latin pēnsiōnem. Doublet of pigione, which was inherited.
From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).
From Latin imāginem (“image, imitation”), from Proto-Italic *imā (“copy”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym- (“copy”). Doublet of imago, and also the now-archaic mania.
First attested 14th century. From Latin aeternus, from an earlier form aeviternus, derived from aevum (“time; age”).
From Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.
From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.
Learned borrowing from Renaissance Latin dictiōnārium.
Borrowed from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”). The nonstandard pronunciation with -é- might be due to influence of entrare.
Borrowed from Latin varius (“diverse, various”), whence also Italian vaio, an inherited doublet.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin correspondēre, from Latin cum + respondeō.

Inherited from Latin scamnum, from Proto-Italic *skaβnom, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ-no-m, from *skabʰ- (“to hold up”). Cognate with Spanish escaño, Galician and Portuguese escano, Romanian scaun, Sanskrit स्कम्भ (skambhá).
From Latin ūnicus, from ūnus; see also -ico.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin habituāre.
From Latin incognitus, equivalent to in- + cognito.
Learned borrowing from Latin cibus. Contrast Portuguese cevo and Spanish cebo (“bait”).
From lungo + -ezza; cognate with Piedmontese longhëssa.
Unadapted borrowing from English bed and breakfast.
Borrowed from French fonctionner. Cognate with Piedmontese funsioné.
From Late Latin fructa, from Latin fructus.
From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τρᾰγῳδῐ́ᾱ (trăgōidĭ́ā), from τρᾰ́γος (trắgos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Borrowed from Latin trāns (“across, on the far side, beyond”). Doublet of tra- and tras-, which were inherited.
From Late Latin valōrem, from Latin valeō.
Borrowed from Latin triumphus, from Old Latin triumpus, via Etruscan *𐌈𐌓𐌉𐌀𐌌𐌐𐌄 (*θriampe), ultimately from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos, “thriambos, a hymn to Dionysus”).
From Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίνειν (krínein, “to decide”).
Borrowed from Latin architectus. Non-etymological /e/ perhaps by analogy with tetto (“roof”).
Inherited from Latin iam (“already, now”). Cognate with Portuguese já and Spanish ya.
From Latin prīncipem (“chief”) (compare principio (“principle”) from the meaning "first").
From Ancient Greek νευρο- (neuro-), combining form of νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”).
From Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion) "parenthetic addition, episode", neuter of ἐπεισόδιος (epeisódios) "following upon the entrance". Cognate with Piedmontese episòdi.
From Latin carbōnem (“charcoal; coal”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker (“to burn”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin carbōnium.
From Latin clāvem, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, of ultimately Proto-Indo-European origin.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obiectum.

Learned borrowing from Latin vēritātem, in this form probably a semi-learned term which was altered based on the Latin etymology. The older, now obsolete forms vertà, vertade, and vertate were inherited.
From the verb governare or from Latin gubernum. Compare Portuguese governo, Spanish gobierno.
Learned borrowing from Latin grātia (“favour/favor; goodwill; charm”).
From ferro- + via, a calque of German Eisenbahn.
Inherited from Old Italian, from Old Occitan ambaissada, from Gaulish ambaxtos.

Probably from a- + mazza (“club, baton”) + -are, or alternatively possibly related to Latin mactāre, through a Vulgar Latin root *mactiāre, although this is less likely. Compare Sicilian ammazzari, Spanish mazar, Portuguese maçar, Occitan massar, Romansh mazzar, Venetan masar, Friulian maçâ, Istriot masà. See also archaic Italian mattare.
Inherited from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.
Borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”) after the humorism theory.
From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).
From French hydrogène. By surface analysis, idro- (“water”) + -geno (“producer”).
From New Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “light-bearing”).
Borrowed from Latin quiētus. Doublet of cheto, which was inherited.
From Latin porticus. Doublet of portego.
From Vulgar Latin Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, and Portuguese fada; French fée; Spanish hada.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).
Borrowed from Late Latin abecedārium, noun use of the neuter form of abecedārius (“pertaining to the alphabet”).
From Ancient Greek γαμέτης (gamétēs, “husband”), from γαμέω (gaméō, “I marry”).
Borrowed from Latin tomus, from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius, from Latin sēcrētus. By surface analysis, segreto (“secret”) + -ario (“-ary”).
Inherited from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs.
From Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).
From Latin Deus, from deus, from earlier *dẹ̄vos, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós. Cognate with English deity.

From Latin Lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).
From Latin Maximus, from maximus (“greatest”), superlative form of magnus (“great, big”).

Ultimately from Latin Padus, perhaps borrowed in this form from some Gallo-Italic variety to judge by the loss of /-d-/. On the other hand, should one assume that said loss occurred (irregularly) in Tuscany, the sound-changes from that point onward would be fairly straightforward: /ˈpa.o/ > /ˈpaw/ > /ˈpɔ/.
Borrowed from French boutique. Doublet of bottega.
From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.
From Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé.
From Latin potentia. By surface analysis, potere + -enza.
From Latin trāductiō, trāductiōnis (“transferring, translation”, literally “leading across”), from trādūcō (“to lead across”), from trāns (“across”) + dūcō (“to lead”).
From Latin austērus, from Ancient Greek αὐστηρός (austērós).
Derived from Late Latin creātūra, from Latin creō.
Borrowed from Latin praeferre, with a change in conjugation.
Borrowed from Latin cancrum. Compare the doublet granchio (“crab”), inherited through a Vulgar Latin diminutive form.
From Latin prēnsus, variant of prehensus.

From Old French bordel (“small hut, cabin; brothel”), diminutive of bord, from Medieval Latin bordellum, from Frankish *bord (“board”), from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board, table”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰr̥dʰ-o- (“board”), suffixed zero-grade form of *bʰer-edʰ- (“to cut”), suffixed form of *bʰer- (“to carve, cut, split, rub”).
Inherited from Late Latin iectāre, from Latin iactāre. Cognate with Sicilian jittari.
Inherited from Latin vīvus (“alive”, “living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
From Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ukos, derived from the root *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare French peu, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco.
Latinization of earlier farraggine, from Latin farrāginem. Doublet of fraina.
Borrowed from Latin reus (“defendant, accused”). Cognate to rio (“bad”), inherited from the same source.
Borrowed from English nabla, from Ancient Greek νάβλα (nábla).
Borrowed from English microchip, from micro- + chip.

Origin uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin cauma, from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, heat of the sun”). Compare Late Latin caumāre (“to rest during the heat (of the day), to siesta”), Sursilvan Romansh cauma (“resting place for livestock, especially during the noon heat”). If the Italian (and Ibero-Romance) word calma originally referred to the heat of the sun, especially around noon (and later to quiet during this time of the day), it may have been influenced by words like Latin calor (“heat”) and cal(i)dus (“hot”), accounting for cal- instead of the expected cau-. Compare also Proto-Germanic *kalmaz (“frozenness, cold”).

From the variant ciriegia, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin. Alternatively from ciliegio, ciriegio (Tuscan), from Late Latin ceresus, from Latin cerasus. See also cerasa. In modern, Tuscan-based Italian, this word underwent hypercorrection twice: * Tuscan hypercorrects intervocalic /r/ to intervocalic /l/ by mistakenly assuming that ⟨cer-⟩ /t͡ʃer/ is a Lombard pronunciation, compare garea, galea → galera; * and ⟨-sa⟩ /za/ → ⟨-gia⟩ /d͡ʒa/, assuming again that ⟨-sa⟩ /za/ is a Lombard pronunciation.
From the Tuscan ciriegio, from Late Latin ceresus, from Latin cerasus.
From Latin rūctus. By surface analysis, deverbal from ruttare + -o.
From Latin hordeum (see there for cognates), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”). Compare Sicilian oriu.
Inherited from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos). Doublet of dattilo.
From Latin chele, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ).
Borrowed from Old French sovent, from Latin subinde. See French souvent.
Derived from Latin thermae, plural of therma.
From Latin rāpa, neuter plural of rāpum, reinterpreted as a feminine singular. Compare French rave, Venetan rava.
From Late Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós, “song sung to a harp, performance on a stringed instrument”), from ψάλλω (psállō, “to pluck an instrument”).
Inherited from Latin bonus. Doublet of bonus, a later borrowing.
From Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos).
Borrowed from Spanish recluta, from French recrue, from Latin recrēscere.
Borrowed from Latin hostia. Compare Spanish hostia.

Inherited from Latin posita, feminine singular of positus, past participle of pōnō (“to put”). Originally, "post for horses or for mooring ships", then "stopping place for coaches on a journey, way station". Doublet of posta (feminine past participle of porre).
From Latin Mārcus, from an earlier adjectival form *martcus (“pertaining to Mars”), from the name of the deity Mārs.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin ictus (“a blow”), from the expression ictus apoplecticus.
Learned borrowing from Latin artēria, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā).
Learned borrowing from Latin pecūnia, derived from pecū (“cattle”).
Borrowed from Latin prō (“in front of”).
From Latin semestris (“six months”), from sex (“six”) + mensis (“month”).
Borrowed from Latin custōdia, a noun derived from custōs (“guardian”).
Borrowed from Latin terreus (“earthy”). By surface analysis, terr(a) (“ground, earth”) + -eo (“-ous”, derivational suffix).
From Latin parāre, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).
Learned borrowing from Latin isthmus, from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck”).
From forca (“gardening fork”) + -etta (diminutive suffix). Compare French fourchette. Sense four is calqued from French.
From Latin praestigium. Cognate with Catalan prestigi, French prestige, Portuguese prestígio, Spanish prestigio.
From tèle- + -scòpio, influenced by Ancient Greek τηλεσκόπος (tēleskópos, “far-seeing”). Coined by Italian polymath Galileo Galilei in 1611.
Inherited from Latin būstum (“burial mound, tomb”). The semantic shift from “tomb” to “bust” happened via the meaning of “sepulchral statue”.
Borrowed from French touriste, from English tourist.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).
Borrowed from Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos). Doublet of tuono.
From Latin apertūra. The sense of "aperture" was a later learned development. Doublet of ouverture.
From Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.
Inherited from Latin nucem. Cognate with Sicilian nuci.
From Late Latin tortūra, from Latin tortus, passive perfect participle of torqueō.
From Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).
Inherited from Latin clārus. Compare Albanian qartë.
Borrowed from French avantage, with rebracketing.
Inherited from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus (“circle”). Compare Catalan anell, French anneau, Portuguese anel, Spanish anillo.
Borrowed from French dame. Doublet of donna.
From Latin ascia (“axe”). In spite of the similar pronunciation, unrelated to French hache, ultimately from Frankish *happjā (“axe, hatchet”).
Either: * From Medieval Latin accostāre, from ac- (“towards”) + costa (“side”) or * From accosto (“near”) + -are. Cognate with English accoster and Spanish acostar.
Borrowed from Latin fāma, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂-mā-, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).
From Old French lot, from Frankish *hlot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.
Learned borrowing from Latin cellula (17th century).
Inherited from Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos).
From Latin laudem, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lēwt-, *lēwdʰ- (“song, sound”), from *lēw- (“to sound, resound, sing out”).
From Latin taenĭa, from Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía, “ribbon, tape”).
From Latin maiōrem /majjoːrɛ̃/, accusative case of maior, from Proto-Italic *magjōs, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂yós, from *méǵh₂s (“big”, “great”).
From Latin fictiōnem, crossed with fingere. Probably a semi-learned term. First attested 13th century.
From abbronzare (“to tan”) + -si (“oneself”, enclitic reflexive pronoun).
Borrowed from French tailleur. Compare Piedmontese tajeur. Doublet of tagliatore.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin spōnsālicius.
Borrowed from French jardin, of Germanic origin (compare Franconian gardo, German Garten).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek αὐτοψία (autopsía, “seeing with one's own eyes”), derived from αὐτός (autós, “self”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “sight”).
From delicato + -ezza; cognate with Piedmontese dlicadëssa.

Borrowed from Latin grātiōsus (“agreeable, popular”), from grātia (“grace”) + -ōsus (“-y, -ous”). By surface analysis, grazia + -oso. Cognate to English gracious, French gracieux, Norman grâcieux, Romanian grațios, Spanish and Portuguese gracioso, Catalan graciós.
From Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós).
From Latin dēvōtus (“vowed, promised, dedicated”), from dēvoveō (“to vow, offer”).
Unadapted borrowing from English governance. There have been attempts to Italianize it into governanza, but the suffix -anza is felt as diminishing its status in formal context.
Borrowed from Latin theca (16th century), from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). Doublet of the inherited tega.
From Latin arāneus (“spider”), related to arānea (“spider”).
From Late Latin vapōrōsus (“full of steam”).
From Latin corvus, from Proto-Italic *korwos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂wós.
From Latin āsiāticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιατικός (Asiatikós).
Borrowed from Latin hēmisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion).
Borrowed from French pistole, from Czech píšťala (“firearm”, literally “tube, pipe”).
From Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstus (“festive”).
Variant of pellegrino, from Latin peregrīnus.
Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀβουλία (aboulía).
Borrowed from Latin inclūsus. Cf. chiuso.
From tessere + -tura. Compare Spanish tejedura, Portuguese tecedura, Romanian țesătură, Friulian tiessidure.

From Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Portuguese tenda, Spanish tienda, French tente, Friulian tinde, Romanian tindă, English tent.
From amaro (“bitter”) + -etto (diminutive suffix), ultimately from Latin amārus.
From Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).
Borrowed from Portuguese fluminense, derived from Classical Latin flūmen (“river”).
Inherited from Latin post merīdiem (“after noon”).
From Latin talpa (“mole”). Doublet of topo.
From Latin nebula, through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nebla. Compare Sicilian negghia, Venetan nebia, Spanish niebla, Romanian negură and Aromanian negurã. Doublet of nebula, which was borrowed.
From Latin malva, of Semitic origin.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cavalier (cf. also Old French chevalier), from Late Latin caballārius. See cavallo + -iere. Doublet of cavallaio.
From Latin gemellus, diminutive of geminus, from Proto-Italic *jemanos, from Proto-Indo-European *yemH-. Compare French jumeau, Portuguese gêmeo, Romanian geamăn, Spanish gemelo.
From Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).
Inherited from Latin palea, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).
Borrowed from Latin pȳramis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís).
From Latin cui. Compare Sicilian cui.
From Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”). Compare Romanian săptămână.
From Latin praeda, from earlier praeheda, from prae- + Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to hold”).
Borrowed from Old French loge, from Medieval Latin laubĭa, from Frankish *laubijā.
Borrowed from French pieuvre, ultimately from Latin polypus, Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous).
From Late Latin camisia, from Transalpine Gaulish, of Germanic origin, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi.
From Old French sidre, from Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σῑ́κερᾰ (sī́keră).
Borrowed from Latin rogus, from Proto-Italic *rogos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-.
Inherited from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-. Doublet of the borrowing corpus.
Inherited from Latin scāla (“stair, staircase, ladder”).
Borrowed from Latin thallus, from Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “young shoot, twig”).
From Latin hymēn (“hymen”), from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”). For the other meaning Borrowed from Latin hymenaeus, from Ancient Greek ὑμέναιος (huménaios).
Borrowed from Latin sapientia, from the verb sapiō (“to know”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abnōrmem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin acūsticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós).
Borrowed from Latin addictus and adapted to native detto.
From Albania + -ese. Cognate with Sicilian arbanisi.
Borrowed from Latin ambientem, present active participle of ambiō (“surround”).
From Latin ambulante, ambulantem, singular of ambulans (“traveling”).
Inherited from Latin vīcus, from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“village, household”).
From Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”).
From Ancient Greek ὑδρο- (hudro-), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”).
Borrowed from Old French cosin, cousin, from Latin cōnsobrīnus. Doublet of consobrino.
From French guépard, from Italian gattopardo.
Inherited from Latin pecora, neuter plural of pecus (“cattle”), from pecū, from Proto-Indo-European *peḱu- (“livestock, domestic animals”). Displaced ovis, which would've yielded either ove or uove.

From Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin. Compare Portuguese cavalo, Asturian caballu, Galician cabalo, Dalmatian caval, Catalan cavall, French cheval, Spanish caballo, Romanian cal, Corsican cavallu, Sardinian cabaddu, Sicilian cavaḍḍu.
From calcolare + -tore; cf. also Latin calculator.
From Latin cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma).
Inherited from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Italic *wrād-mo-, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
Inherited from Latin soror (nominative) via loss of /-r/ and then adjustment of /-o/ to the more typical (for feminine nouns) /-a/.
Borrowed from French ozone, from German Ozon, from Ancient Greek ὄζω (ózō).
From Latin Pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ).
Borrowed from English amphetamine, shortened form of alpha-methylphenethylamine.
From Medieval Latin cursīvus (probably a semi-learned borrowing), from Latin cursus.
From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion).
Borrowed from Latin siliceus. Doublet of the inherited serizzo.
Metathesized from earlier sucido, from Latin sūcidus (“oily”, “greasy”). Doublet of sozzo.
Borrowed from Latin furia. Doublet of foia, which was inherited.
Borrowed from French embarcadère, from Spanish embarcadero.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperītīvus, from Late Latin apertīvus, from Latin aperiō, and partly from French apéritif.
From minestra (“soup”, ultimately from Latin ministrō) + -one (augmentative suffix).
Dissimilation from Latin peregrīnus. Cognate to Sicilian piḍḍigrinu, English peregrine (“wandering”) and pilgrim.
Borrowed from Latin pōlypus, from Doric Greek πώλυπος (pṓlupos) (compare Attic πολύπους (polúpous)).
Borrowed from French côtelette, from Middle French costelette (literally “little rib”). Doublet of costoletta.
From Late Latin albōrem, from Latin albus (“white”).
From Latin strūthiō, from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn).
Inherited from Latin ōricula, variant of auricula. Doublet of auricola, a borrowing from Latin.
From Ancient Greek στέρνον (stérnon, “chest, breastbone, heart”).
Learned borrowing from Latin naevus, from earlier gnaevus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁iwós (“native”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget”). Doublet of neo.
Borrowed from Old French roche, from Early Medieval Latin rocca, of uncertain origin. Doublet of rocca.
From Latin phāsiānus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós).
From Latin maiālis, from the goddess Maia.
From Latin rēnem, of uncertain origin.
From costola (“rib”) + -etta (diminutive suffix). Doublet of cotoletta.
From sugo + -oso, or possibly from Latin sūcōsus, from sūcus. Doublet of succoso.
From cavolo + fiore. Compare French chou-fleur, English cauliflower.
Derived from Late Latin caulus, from Latin caulis,, through a southern Italian language. Possibly borrowed from Neapolitan cavolo or Sicilian cavulu. Doublet of caule.
Inherited from Latin laurus, with the agglutination of a definite article to the beginning. Doublet of lauro. Compare Sicilian aḍḍauru.

A syncope of earlier pretosemolo, with metathesis from petrosemolo, from a cross of Latin petroselīnum and sēmen (thus "stone seed") as in Sardinian perdusèmene. The Latin word borrowed from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon), from πέτρα (pétra, “stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”).
Borrowed from French stère, from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”).

From Late Latin sagmārius, saumārius, salmārius, from Late Latin sagma (“pack saddle”), from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma). Doublet of somiere. The obsolete English word summer (“pack-horse”) is borrowed from the same source.
From Late Latin mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”).
From Vulgar Latin *prūnea, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon). Cognate with Sicilian prunu.
From Medieval Latin ribes (“currant”), from Arabic رِيبَاس (rībās, “Syrian rhubarb; currant”), from Persian ریواس (rivâs, “rhubarb”), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *(h)rabā́š (“rhubarb; fennel”).
From catena (“chain, bond”) + -accio, or from Late Latin catēnāceum, from Latin catēna.
Learned borrowing from Latin gigās, from Ancient Greek γίγᾱς (gígās, “giant”).
From Latin rūsticus, derived from Proto-Italic *rowos (“country, countryside”).
From guancia (“cheek”) + -ale. Compare Proto-West Germanic *wangārī (“pillow”), from Proto-West Germanic *wangā (“cheek”).
Inherited from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”).
Borrowed from French ragoût, from Middle French ragoûter (“to awaken the appetite”), from goût (“taste”), from Latin gustus. See also gusto (“taste”) and its derivations.
Borrowed from Neapolitan vongola, from Latin conchula, from concha. Displaced Old Italian gongola.
From Latin nympha or nymphe (“nymph”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “young woman, nymph”).
Learned borrowing from Latin nū̆cleus (“kernel, core”).
From Latin nārrātīvus, from nārrō (“to narrate”).
From Latin nātīvus. Doublet of naïf.
Borrowed from Old French frape, of uncertain origin.
From navigare + -zione, or borrowed from Latin nāvigātiōnem.
From nazione + -ale; cf. New Latin nātiōnālis.
Learned borrowing from Latin negātiōnem. By surface analysis, negare (“deny”) + -zione (“-tion”).
Borrowed from Latin negligentia, variant of neglegentia.
Borrowed from Latin nēquitia, derived from nēquam (“worthless”).
Borrowed from French brevet, diminutive of bref.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *assus, from Classical Latin as.
Borrowed from French automatique. By surface analysis, auto- + -matico or automato + -ico.
From avanzare (“to advance”) + -ata (suffix expressing an instance of something).
From Latin capitium, probably through a diminutive Vulgar Latin form *capitiulum or *capitiolum.
From Late Latin Iācomus, dialect variant of Latin Iācōbus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Ἰακώβ (Iakṓb), from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿăqōḇ).
From Late Latin ballistra, from ballista, Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra).
Borrowed from Old French batel. Compare Spanish, Galician, and Portuguese batel.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus. Synchronicallty bis- (“twice”) + cotto (“baked, cooked”). Doublet of biscuit.

Borrowed from French bleu (“blue”) from Middle French bleu, from Old French blou, bleve (“pallid, wan, discoloured/discolored, blue”), from Frankish *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue, yellowish-gray”). Doublet of biavo.
From Latin bovem. Doublet of bue. Cognate with Sicilian voi.
From boxe + -are, on the model of English to box, French boxer.
Deverbal from bramare (“to long, yearn for”) + -a.
Deverbal from posare + -a, or inherited from Latin pausa.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin mīrābilia, neuter plural form of the adjective mīrābilis (“wonderful, marvelous”). Doublet of meraviglia.
From Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos).
From rosso + -astro, a calque of French rougeâtre.
Learned borrowing from Latin cadūcu(m), from Latin cadūcus.
From Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos).
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).
From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin quāglum/ *coāglum, from Latin coāgulum. Doublet of coagulo, a borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Latin canōrus. First attested in the 16th century.
From French casino, itself from Italian.
Inherited from Latin capsa. Doublet of capsa.
From New Latin Cavia, from Old Galician-Portuguese çavia (“the spiny rat”), from Old Tupi saujá. Compare Portuguese sauiá.
Learned borrowing from Latin celer, celerem.
Inherited from Latin cippus. Doublet of cippo, which was borrowed.
Borrowed from French marne, of Gaulish origin.
Learned borrowing from Latin coetus (“group, society”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “about, around”).
Borrowed from French milliard, from a change in suffix of million.
Inherited from Late Latin claustrum (“portion of monastery closed off to laity”), from Latin claustrum (“place shut in, bar, bolt, enclosure”).
Inherited from Latin faba, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”).
Borrowed from Latin cīvīlis, from cīvis (“citizen”).
From Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).
From Latin cilium, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel-yo-m, which is derived from *ḱel- (“to cover”).
Borrowed from Latin circus. Doublet of the now-archaic cerco (“circle, circus”), which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus. Compare the inherited doublets diritto and dritto.
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin īsicia, plural of īsicium (“minced meat”), from īnsicium < Latin īnsecō (“cut up”). Compare Spanish chicha. Alternatively, from a syncope of carniccia.
From Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros).
From Latin cȳmatium, from Ancient Greek κυμάτιον (kumátion, “small wave”).
From Late Latin cimelium, from Ancient Greek κειμήλιον (keimḗlion, “relic”).
From Ancient Greek κινητικός (kinētikós, “one who puts in motion”).
From cinta + -are; cognate with Friulian centâ, Piedmontese cinté.
Borrowed from Latin cippus. Doublet of ceppo, which was inherited.
From New Latin cirrhosis, from Ancient Greek κῐρρός (kĭrrhós) and -ωσις (-ōsis) (Italian -osi).
From Latin olīva, from Etruscan 𐌄𐌋𐌄𐌉𐌅𐌀 (eleiva) or from Proto-Hellenic *elaíwā (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀨𐀷 (e-ra-wa), Ancient Greek ἐλαίᾱ (elaíā)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁loywom.
Borrowed from French clinique, ultimately from Ancient Greek κλινική (klinikḗ).
From Latin arista. Compare the borrowed doublet arista.
From Latin cognātus (“related by blood”), from cum (“with”) + nātus (“born”).
From Latin collātiōnem (“putting together, meeting”). Originally it was the name of the meal that monks ate after the evening meeting. Doublet of collazione.
From Latin passer remodeled as a third-declension noun, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *p(e)t-tro- (“who flies, bird”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”).
From a derivative of Latin gāvia, like Spanish gaviota.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *niblus, syncopated form of Latin nibulus, from an alteration of Latin milvus.
From Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós).
Inherited from Latin iuncus. Cognate with Sicilian juncu.
From Ancient Greek οὐρία (ouría, a kind of duck).
From Latin cicōnia, derived from Proto-Indo-European *kekoh₂n-, from the root *keh₂n- (“to sing”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan austor, from Vulgar Latin *acceptōrem, modification of Latin accipiter (“hawk”). Unlikely to derive from Latin astŭrem (“type of hawk”), considering its stress position.
From Latin emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρος (émplastros).
From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptismus, baptismum, from Ancient Greek βαπτισμός (baptismós). Doublet of battismo.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin democratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρατίᾱ (dēmokratíā). By surface analysis, demo- + -crazia.
Inherited from Latin tēctum (“roof”). Compare French toit, Portuguese teto, Spanish techo.
Latinization of older cotornice, inherited from Latin cōturnīcem; attested from the late 13th or early 14th century.
From fischio (“whistle”) + -one. From the sound they make when flying.
Inherited from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos). Doublet of golfo.
From Latin cōmicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós).
From Late Latin commūnālis, from Latin commūnis.
From Latin cōnus, from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos).
From Late Latin cognōscentia, from Latin cognōscēns.
Borrowed from Old French conté, from Latin comitātus. Doublet of contado. The modern sense of an administrative division is a semantic loan from English county.
Borrowed from French émou, from English emu.
Variant of pallio, from Latin pallium (“cloak; coverlet”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula, which was borrowed. Compare Sicilian cucchia.
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).
From Ancient Greek ἀναισθησία (anaisthēsía), from ἀν- (an-) "not" + αἴσθησις (aísthēsis) "sensation".
Learned borrowing from Latin ānulāris (“annular, ring-shaped”).

Borrowed from Spanish brindar, from brindis (“toast”), from German bring dir's, dialectal contraction of bringe dir es, probably introduced by German mercenaries in the 16th c. Compare Portuguese brinde and Italian brindisi.
Borrowed from Late Latin clausūra, from Latin clausus, past participle of claudō (“to close, to shut”). See also the inherited doublet chiusura.
Borrowed from Latin coāgulāre. Compare the doublet cagliare.
From Latin compāginem, formation of compāgēs (whence compage).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *conquista (“conquest”). Compare Spanish conquista, French conquête. By surface analysis, conquistare (“to conquer”) + -a.
Borrowed from Late Latin contentāre, derived from contentus.
Borrowed from Latin culminem (first attested 16th century). Doublet of the inherited colmo.
From Late Latin dēcapitāre, present infinitive of dēcapitō, by surface analysis, dē- (“off”) + caput (“head”) + -āre, literally “to de-head”.
Borrowed from Latin dēfōrmis (“deformed, ugly”), from dē + fōrma (“shape, form”).
Borrowed from Late Latin distorsiōnem, from Latin distortiōnem.
Borrowed from French drainer, from English drain.
Borrowed from French émulsion, from New Latin ēmulsiōnem, based on Latin ēmulgeō (“to milk out, extract”).
Borrowed from Latin fōmentāre, from fōmentum.
From Latin generum, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.
Borrowed from New Latin gravitāre, from Latin gravitās.
Unadapted borrowing from English megawatt. By surface analysis, mega- + watt.
Unadapted borrowing from English megavolt. By surface analysis, mega- + volt.
From Latin lapidem (“stone”). Doublet of lapis.
Borrowed from Spanish lindo. Doublet of limpido.
From pelo + -are or from Latin pilāre (“to deprive of hair”).
From Latin praecīsus (“shortened”), from praecīdō (“to shorten”).
From Russian коза́к (kozák), from Old East Slavic козак (kozak), itself of Turkic origin. Doublet of kazako.
From Ancient Greek κόσμησις (kósmēsis, “an adorning”), from κοσμέω (kosméō, “to order, arrange, adorn”).
Either from Latin prīvus or a short participle form corresponding to privato.
From Vulgar Latin *mina, Gaulish *meina (see also Welsh mwyn, Middle Irish míanach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).
From Latin ōrnāmentum (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from ōrnō (“to equip, adorn”).
Borrowed from Latin rēgālis. Doublet of reale, which came via Old French.
From remo + -are. Compare Spanish and Portuguese remar, French ramer.
Borrowed from Late Latin syncope, from Ancient Greek συγκοπή (sunkopḗ), from σύν (sún) + κόπτω (kóptō, “strike, cut off”).
Borrowed from Late Latin templāris, derivate from Latin templum.
From Latin testimōnium, derived from testis.
From Latin trāmitem (“path”). Cognate to Catalan tràmit, Portuguese trâmite and Spanish trámite.
From a diminutive of Latin cutis (“skin”).
Borrowed from Latin lynx, whence also Doublet of lonza (inherited).
Inherited from Latin phōca f, from Ancient Greek φώκη f (phṓkē). Compare French phoque m.
From Latin suī (“of oneself”) + -cida (“murderer”), on the example of omicida.
Borrowed from French dard (“javelin”), from Old French dart, from Frankish *darōþu.
From Latin crater (“basin”), from Ancient Greek κρατήρ (kratḗr, “mixingbowl, wassail-bowl”).
Borrowed from Middle French portier, from Late Latin portārius (“doorkeeper”, “gatekeeper”). By surface analysis, porta (“door”) + -iere (“-er”, agent noun suffix).
From mignatta (“leech”) + -aio (suffix denoting an occupation). The zoological sense derived from the archaic belief that the bird fed on leeches.
From Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).
Inherited from Latin tangentem, borrowed in the mathematical senses.
Borrowed from German Kren, from a Slavic source, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xrěnъ; compare Russian хрен (xren), Serbo-Croatian хре̏н/hrȅn.
Inherited from Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).
From Late Latin or Juridical Latin criminālis (“criminal”), from Latin crīmen (“verdict; crime”).
Borrowed from Latin crypta, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Doublet of grotta, which Italian inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).
Borrowed from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos).
From Latin Christiānus, from Χρῑστός (Khrīstós, “Christ, Anointed [One]”) + Latin suffix -ānus. Doublet of cretino.
From Latin Chrīstus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós), proper-noun use of χριστός (khristós, “the anointed one”), calqued after Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ, “anointed”).
From Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “gathering of people or place of gathering”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).
From Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
From Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos).
From necro- (“necro-”, “death”) + -filia (“-philia”, suffix indicating liking or love of something).
From Latin hūmōrem. Doublet of humour.
Unadapted borrowing from English microvolt. By surface analysis, micro- + volt.
From Late Latin bibliothēcārius (“librarian”). By surface analysis, biblioteca (“library”) + -ario.
Inherited from Latin mola, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”).
Borrowed from Latin īnfāntem. Doublet of the inherited fante.
Inherited from Latin grānum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
Learned borrowing from Latin scēna, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).
Inherited from Latin crusta, from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).
Borrowed from English crucial, itself from French crucial (“cruciform”).

From Vulgar Latin *cunla, syncopated form of cūnula, diminutive of Latin cūna, cūnae (“cradle”), from Proto-Italic *koinā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoyneh₂, derived from the root *ḱey- (“to be lying down; to settle”). Doublet of cuna.
From Latin chȳmus, from Ancient Greek χῡμός (khūmós).
From passare + -aggio, or from Old French passage.
Learned borrowing from Latin cumulus. Doublet of cumolo, and possibly mucchio.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rubīnus.
Borrowed from Latin artemīsia, from Ancient Greek ἀρτεμῑσία (artemīsía), from Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis, “Artemis, the goddess”).
Unadapted borrowing from English megabit. By surface analysis, mega- + bit.
From Latin miserum, of uncertain origin. Possibly a borrowing.
From Latin verbum (“word, verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from root *werh₁- (“to speak, to say”) + extension *-dʰ-.
Borrowed from Lombardic milzi, from Proto-Germanic *miltiją, akin to English milt, German Milz, Danish milt etc.
Learned borrowing from Latin custōdem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, hide”).
From Late Latin scholāris, from Latin schola.
From Vulgar Latin *papāverum, from Latin papāver (“poppy”).
From Medieval Latin jacintus, from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers; a blue precious stone”).
Borrowed from Latin digitālis. Doublet of ditale, which was inherited.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pervinca, from Latin pervincīre (“to entwine, bind, fetter”), from per- (“thoroughly”) and vincīre (“to bind, fetter”).
Borrowed from Latin crassus. Doublet of grasso.
From Latin rānunculus. By surface analysis, rana (“frog”) + -uncolo.
Borrowed from Latin āthlēta, from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs).
From Latin Titius: the name Tizio is usually the first placeholder name, which caused it to become a generic word for "a person".
The feminized version of the masculine ragazzo (“boy; boyfriend”) from Vulgar Latin *ragatius, from Ancient Greek ῥάκος (rhákos, “rag, tatter”, suggesting the clothing).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitātem, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), from Classical Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ālis. Doublet of realità, which is a learned borrowing.
From Late Latin *bacius, formed from *bombacius, a variant of Latin bombyx.
From danzare (“to dance”) + -tore (“-er”, agent noun suffix).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin datium, by-form of Medieval Latin dātiō (“the act of giving”).
From Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos).
From earlier esemplo, essemplo, probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin exemplum, derived from Latin eximō (“to take out, take away”). Compare the inherited doublet scempio.
Borrowed from Latin fēlīnus (“feline”), from fēlēs (“cat”).
Probably borrowed from Latin patriarchātus ultimately from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs).
From capo- + luogo, calque of French chef-lieu.
From Latin tītiō (“firebrand”). Compare among others French tison, Spanish tizón and Romanian tăciune.
From Late Latin annuālis, from Latin annus.
From Latin illustris (“bright, shining, brilliant, lustrous; clear, lucid; illustrious, distinguished, famous”), from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).
From Latin hōrologium, from Koine Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).
From earlier *stacione, from Latin statiōnem. Doublet of stazzo, stazzone, stazio, and stazione, the first two of which were also inherited from Latin, while the latter two were borrowed.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pascua, from Latin pascha (influenced by pascuum, pascua (“grazing”)), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), ultimately from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésakh, “Passover”). The surname was given to someone who was born this day.
Borrowed from Spanish guerrilla. By surface analysis, guerra (“war”) + -iglia.
From annuo, or borrowed from Late Latin annuārius, from Latin annus.
From Latin quotīdiānus, from quot (“as often as”) + diēs (“day”).
Learned borrowing from Latin diurnus, whence also the inherited doublet giorno.
avanti (“before”) + ieri (“yesterday”) See also French avant-hier.
From oliva or from Vulgar Latin olīvus, from Latin olīva, olīvum.
Borrowed from French dispositif, from Latin dispositus, perfect passive participle of dispōnō.
From New Latin aphēlium, from Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “from, away from”) "from, away from" + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “the Sun”), modeled after apogaeum.
From Latin Graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).
From Latin frātellus, a diminutive of Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
From Latin soror, from a diminutive form or based on the model of fratello. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *swezōr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
From Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιαστής (enthousiastḗs); compare French enthousiaste.

From Late Latin campānia (whence also Spanish campaña, Portuguese and Occitan campanha, French champagne), from campāneus, based on Latin campus (“level field”). Doublet of champagne, borrowed from French.
From Medieval Latin or Late Latin campiōnem, campiōnem (“champion, fighter”), from Frankish *kampijō (or a Lombardic equivalent) from Proto-Germanic *kampijô, based on Latin campus (“level ground”).

From Latin flamma, from Proto-Italic *flāgmā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₂gmeh₂, derived from an extension of the root *bʰel- (“shiny, white”). Compare French flamme, Portuguese chama, Spanish llama.
From Latin fēminīnus, with change of suffix by dissimilation. By surface analysis, femmina (“female”, noun) + -ile.
From Vulgar Latin *visclum, contraction of *visculum, from Latin viscum.
From Medieval Latin mānsum. Compare Catalan mas (“farmhouse”).
Either a latinization of an older term or borrowed from Latin inguen.
Borrowed from Old French flanc (“flank, side”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin ēvangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”). Compare French évangile, Piedmontese vangel, Portuguese evangelho, Spanish evangelio.
From camera (“room”) + -iere. Compare Spanish camarero, Late Latin camerārius (“chamberlain”).
Inherited from Latin cervīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head”) and *weyk- (“to bend”), borrowed in modern senses.
Borrowed from Late Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
