From Latin monasterium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion).
From Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
Borrowed from Late Latin praenotātiōnem, form of praenotātiō.
From Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma, “laborous breathing”).
Borrowed from Old French maniere, from manere.
From paese + -aggio, based on French paysage. Compare also Spanish paisaje, Portuguese paisagem, Piedmontese paisagi, Sicilian pajisaggiu.
From Latin efficāx (“efficacious, effectual, powerful, efficient”).
Borrowed from Latin decennium. Re-analyzable as dieci + -ennio.
From Late Latin, Vulgar Latin -iscus. Cognates: see Proto-Germanic *-iskaz.
From Latin decentem, accusative case form of decēns (“appropriate, fitting”), present active participle of decet (“[it] is fitting”).
From tradizione + -ale; cognate with Piedmontese tradissional/tradissiunal.
From Latin recepta, feminine of receptus (“received”), from perfect passive participle of recipiō (“to receive”). Compare Sicilian rizzetta.
From Latin odōrem, from an archaic form odōs, from Proto-Italic *odōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃édos, derived from the root *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Doublet of aulore and olore.
Borrowed from Late Latin praevīsiōnem, from Latin praevideō.
Borrowed from Latin litterārius, derived from littera (“letter”).
From Late Latin litterālis. By surface analysis, lettera + -ale.
Learned borrowing from Latin stīpendium (“military pay, stipend”).
From Latin extrāneus, possibly through an intermediate adjective *extranearius, or more likely based on the model of Old French estrangier.
From Late Latin Christianismus, from Christus, corresponding to Ancient Greek χρῑστιᾱνισμός (khrīstiānismós). By surface analysis, cristiano (“Christian”) + -esimo (“-ism”).
Borrowed from Latin nebulōsus. Cognate to Italian nebbioso, which is however not a borrowing but an Italian formation.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Slavus, from Late Latin Sclāvus, from Medieval Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. See also the related term schiavo.
From Latin monumentum, possibly a borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin māternitātem.
From Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).
From Late Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).
Learned borrowing from New Latin bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “small staff”), from βακτηρία (baktēría) + -ium.
From Old Italian preite, from Vulgar Latin *previter, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare French prêtre, Romanian preot.
From Old Occitan preguiera, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem. Cognate with Sicilian prijera.

Borrowed from Old Occitan carreira or its variants (compare modern Occitan carrièra, also French carrière), from Late Latin carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare the inherited doublet carraia, now archaic.
From Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “master, lord, ruler, despot”).
Borrowed from Latin gladius, possibly from Gaulish *kladyos (“sword”), from Proto-Celtic *kladiwos (“sword”), from the Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”).
From Latin sociālis (“of or pertaining to companionship; social”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, associate, companion”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”).
From Medieval Latin mūsicālis, derived from Latin mūsica.
From Latin ligāmen (“bandage, band, tie”). Compare Sicilian ligama.
From Classical Latin saxum, from Proto-Italic *saksom, of unknown origin. Compare Portuguese seixo (“pebble”) and Spanish saxo (“stone”).
From Late Latin signāle < signālis, from Latin signum.
Learned borrowing from Latin expressiōnem (“a pressing out”).
Borrowed from Latin affirmātiōnem (“affirmation, declaration”), derived from affirmō (“to affirm, assert”).
From Latin flōreus (“flowery”) + -ale, the noun as a calque of French floréal.
From the older armario, borrowed from Latin armārium.
From Latin exsūctus, past participle of exsūgō, from ex + sūgō. Compare Sicilian asciuttu, Spanish enjuto, Portuguese enxuto, Catalan eixut.
Borrowed from Latin augurium. Related to Old Italian agurio, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin exāmen. Doublet of sciame, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin errōrem. Sense 2 is built from the original Latin sense of errō (“to wander”). By surface analysis, errare + -ore.
Borrowed from Latin extrāneus (“external, foreign; strange”), whence also Italian strano (an inherited doublet).
From elettore + -ale. Cognate to Catalan electoral, French électoral, Portuguese eleitoral, Spanish electoral.
From Latin excellentem (“distinguished”, “excellent”), present active participle of excellō (“to elevate, raise up”).
From Late Latin discursus, from Latin discurrō.
From an alteration, based on its Latin root, of the older disidero, desidero, from Latin dēsīderium.
From dichiarare + -zione, based on Latin dēclārātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin probābilitātem. By surface analysis, probabile + -ità.
Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin periculōsus. By surface analysis, pericolo + -oso.
Borrowed from Latin impatientia. Cognate with Piedmontese impassiensa.
Learned borrowing from Latin patientem, present active participle of patior (“to suffer”).
Deverbal from passeggiare + -o or to walk, stroll + -o. Cognate with Catalan passeig, Portuguese passeio, Spanish paseo, Sicilian passiju.
Borrowed from Latin prŏprietātem. By surface analysis, proprio + -età.
From Latin timōrem. Cf. also Old Italian temore, which was likely altered to reflect the Latin more closely.
From Latin pretium, whence also Italian pregio, a doublet. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”). Cognate with Walloon and French près.
Borrowed from French personnage; persona + -aggio. Compare Piedmontese përsonagi.
Borrowed from Latin horizontem, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
From Latin operārius. By surface analysis, from operare + -aio
Borrowed from Latin numerōsus. By surface analysis, numero + -oso. Compare novero.
Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem, whence also Italian cagione (an inherited doublet).
Borrowed from Late Latin hōrārium. Cognate with Piedmontese orari.
From Latin facienda, neuter plural of faciendus (“that which is to be done”). Doublet of azienda. Cognate with Sicilian facenna.
From Latin facultātem, probably a borrowing.
From raccolto (“harvested”) + -a (“things that are ~”), from Latin -a, neuter plural of -us adjectives, used for substantivization, later reanalyzed as feminine singular, cf. mobilia, etc.

From Latin ratiōnem, whence also razione (a borrowed doublet). The natural outcome would have been razzone [rat'tsone] (which is attested in some archaic works in Roman vernacular); the reason why the modern form shows a g is that Tuscan literates mistook Northern rason as an outcome of non-existent Latin **rasione~**raseone—whose -sj- indeed evolves regularly into tuscan [ʃ]~[ʒ] and non-tuscan [s]<s> (compare fagiolo from Latin phaseolum, and compare the pronunciation of English vision as "vizhun"—indeed, approvvigionare ultimately comes from Latin visionem with the same assimilation of -sj- into a palatal voiced fricative). Compare other terms ending in -gione. Furthermore, the reason why it’s nowadays pronounced with an affricate rather than a fricative (together with all Italian terms having as the corresponding etymological clusters being -tj- or -sj-, or even -cj- through Gallic languages—see crogiolo) is due to hyper-correction of Tuscan gorgia, i.e. the merging of ungeminated fricatives and affricates into the first ones. From Old French bouter (“to strike”), of Germanic origin. Compare Neapolitan vottare and Sicilian vottare.

Borrowed from Latin rōbustus (“hard, solid”, literally “oaken, of oak”), derived from rōbur (“hard oak; hardness”), from ruber (“red”) (for its reddish hardwood), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós, from the root *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Doublet of rubesto.

Attested from ca. 1261. A cross of inherited sempice, semprice with Latin simplicem, from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”) + *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). Compare duplice, molteplice. Partial doublet of scempio.
Inherited from Late Latin iūrāmentum (“oath”). By surface analysis, giurare (“to swear, make an oath”) + -mento (“-ment”).
From Latin dēficientia. Compare Catalan deficiència, Portuguese deficiência, Spanish deficiencia.
Borrowed from Latin intēnsus. Doublet of inteso.
Borrowed from Latin iūstitia. Doublet of giustezza.
Probably from Old French bouton, from the verb bouter, or alternatively possibly from Vulgar Latin *bottonem or *botonus.
From borgo + -ese < Late Latin burgus, or through burgensis. Compare French bourgeois, Spanish burgués, English burgess.
From vita + -ale, or from Latin vītālis.
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primaio, primiero, and premier.
From Latin subterraneus, possibly an adaptation to Italian or semi-learned term.
Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin singulāris. By surface analysis, singolo + -are. Doublet of cinghiale.
Borrowed from French banal, derived from ban (“declaration, announcement”).
From Latin īnsufficientem. Cognate with Friulian insuficient, Piedmontese insuficent.
Perhaps from Latin exsuccus (“sapless, lifeless”), from ex- + succus (“juice, moisture”) (compare exsūcō).
Borrowed from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολαστικός (skholastikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin statiōnem. Doublet of stagione, stazzo, stazzone, and stazio, of which the first three were inherited from Latin, while the last was borrowed.
Borrowed from Latin templum. First attested 14th century.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sānctuārium.
Probably borrowed from Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon), derived from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to make”). Cf. the doublet argano.
From Latin charactērem (““characteristic”, “mark””), from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).
From Late Latin compāniō (nominative form), a calque of Proto-West Germanic *gahlaibō. Doublet of compagnone, which came via the Latin accusative compāniōnem.
Borrowed from Latin sapientem (“discerning, wise”), present active participle of sapiō (“to be wise”). Doublet of saccente.
Learned borrowing from Latin commūnicātiōnem (“sharing, communication”).
Inherited from Late Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput.
Borrowed from Spanish cumplimiento. Doublet of complemento.
From Latin peiōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”).
Borrowed from Latin dēlēgātiōnem, from dēlēgō.
Borrowed from French délétère, from Ancient Greek δηλητήριος (dēlētḗrios, “noxious, deleterious”).
From Latin obēsus, derived from obedō (“to devour”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin reflexiōnem.
From Latin rigidus (“rigid”), from rigeō (“to am stiff”).
From Old Occitan guidar, of Germanic origin; e.g. Frankish *witan, Proto-Germanic *witaną, possibly through a Medieval Latin intermediary. Compare French guider, Spanish guiar.
Probably from Old Occitan esvelhar, from Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre [whence also Old French esveillier], from Latin ēvigilāre.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓κρόπολῐς (ăkrópolĭs). By surface analysis, acro- + -poli.
From Latin stupĕndum, from stupēre. Cognate with Piedmontese stupend.
Inherited from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), from Semitic.
From tras- + curare; cognate with Piedmontese trascuré.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀκτάγωνον (oktágōnon), from ὀκτάγωνος (oktágōnos, “eight-angled”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin opticus, from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós, “of seeing”).
From Latin tabula. Doublet of tabula and tavolo.
Calque of French fantaisiste, from fantasia + -ista.
Borrowed from Late Latin dēlinquentia, derived from Latin dēlinquēns, present participle of dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”).
From Latin dēlīrium, from dēlīrō (“to deviate from the path”).
From Latin minācia (“threat”), a noun based on mināx (“threatening”).

Borrowed from Greek μακάρι (makári, “I wish”), which is derived from Ancient Greek μακάριος (makários, “blessed, happy”). Compare Sicilian macari, Portuguese macar (“although”, conjunction), Spanish maguer (“although”, conjunction) and Romanian măcar (“even”, adverb).
Learned borrowing from Latin miseria (“misery”). By surface analysis, mìsero + -èria.
From s- + cocca (“the notch of an arrow”) + -are.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin effectuāre.
From Ancient Greek θυρεός (thureós, “a large oblong shield”) + -oide.
From Ancient Greek ὑπόφυσις (hupóphusis, “attachment underneath”), from ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature”), from φύω (phúō, “to bring forth”).
Borrowed from French jardinier. By surface analysis, giardino + -iere.
From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus (possibly semi-learned), itself from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

From Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός (euphēmismós), from εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō), from εὔφημος (eúphēmos, “uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φάναι (phánai, “to speak, say”).
Inherited from Old Italian caviaro, from Turkish havyar.
Borrowed from New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”).
From a- + cennare, the latter from Early Medieval Latin cinnāre (“blink”).
From Old French demaine (“holdings”), from Latin dominium.
Borrowed from New Latin cervīcālis, formed from the root of Latin cervīx (“the neck, nape of the neck”) and -ālis (see -ale). By surface analysis, cervice + -ale.
Borrowed from Latin connexiōnem, alternative form of cōnexiō (“junction”, “connection”).
From Ancient Greek γάγγλιον (gánglion, “encysted tumour on a tendon, anything gathered into a ball”).
Inherited from Late Latin iūsum~iōsum, from Classical Latin deorsum.
Borrowed from Latin trigōnometria. Equivalent to trigono + -metria.
From Latin ulmus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”).
Deverbal from squadrare + -a. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *exquadra, from *exquadro, exquadrāre, from Latin ex- + quadrō, from quadrus. Compare French équerre.
From Arabic مَخَازِن pl (maḵāzin), plural of مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “storeroom, storehouse”), noun of place from خَزَنَ (ḵazana, “to store, to stock, to lay up”). Compare Sicilian magasenu.
Borrowed from French communiste. Influenced by comune.
Borrowed from French communisme. Influenced by Italian comune.
From Lombardic zapfo (“plug, tap”), from Proto-Germanic *tappô. Doublet of tappo.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós), derived from ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, spirit”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin temporāneus.
From Latin glāns, glāndem, with change in declension, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂- (“acorn”). Compare French gland, Romanian ghindă.
From ri- + guardare. Compare French regarder.
From riflesso + -ivo, or from Medieval Latin reflexīvus.
Borrowed from Latin dēmōnstrātiōnem, or from dimostrare + -zione.
From Latin daemon, from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn).
Borrowed from Latin daemonium, from Ancient Greek δαιμόνιον (daimónion), diminutive of δαίμων (daímōn, “god, divine power”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vīsīvus, derived from Classical Latin vīsus. Cognate with Piedmontese visiv.
Borrowed from Late Latin visuālis, from Latin visus.
Inherited from Latin trīstitia. By surface analysis, triste + -ezza. Doublet of tristizia, a borrowing from Latin.
From dente + -iera; cognate with Piedmontese dentera.
From ri- + uscire. Compare French réussir, borrowed via riuscita.
Ultimately from Medieval Greek μονόλογος (monólogos, “speaking alone”).

From Latin betulla, diminutive of Gaulish *betua, from Proto-Celtic *betwiyos, *betuyā (“birch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-. Compare Portuguese bétula, Spanish abedul, Catalan bedoll, French bouleau.
Borrowed from Latin dēpilāre. Compare the inherited doublet dipelare.
From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).
From tra- + tenere. Compare Sicilian trattèniri.
From Latin trānsversus. Compare French travers.
From Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos).
From Spanish caimán, from Kari'na acayouman.
From Latin cardamōmum, from Ancient Greek καρδάμωμον (kardámōmon).
Inherited from Latin lectūra. By surface analysis, leggere + -tura.
Calque of English interview, from inter- + vista. Compare Spanish and Portuguese entrevista.
Borrowed from Latin cyta, from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos).
From Medieval Latin conditiōnālis (“conditional”), from conditiō (“condition”).
Borrowed from English gecko, from Malay gekok (also written geˀkok or gĕkoq).

Borrowed from English alligator, from Early Modern English alligater, alligarta, aligarto, alegarto, alagarto, from Spanish el lagarto (“the lizard”), from Latin lacertus (“lizard”). Doublet of lucertola (“lizard”).
Borrowed from Late Latin inconvenientis. By surface analysis, in- + conveniente.
From Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed, a sowing”).
Borrowed from Latin reductiōnem, or from ridurre + -zione.

From *cranclu(m), accusative singular of Vulgar Latin *cranclus, by metathesis and syncope from a Late Latin *cancrulus (compare attested Medieval Latin cancrulus), a diminutive of Latin cancer (“crab”). The Latin derives from Proto-Italic *kankros, dissimilation of *karkros (“enclosure”) (because the pincers of a crab form a circle), from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). See also the doublet cancro (“cancer”).
From Late Latin indiānus, from India.
From Latin paupertātem. By surface analysis, povero + -tà.
From Late Latin indiscussus. By surface analysis, in- + discusso.
From Late Latin indistīnctus, from in- + distīnctus, perfect passive participle of Latin distinguō. By surface analysis, in- + distinto.
From Late Latin inexperientia, from in- + experientia. By surface analysis, in- + esperienza.
Borrowed from Latin īnfāmia (“infamy”), from īnfāmis (“infamous”), from in- (“not”) + fāma (“fame, renown”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īnfernālis.
From Latin īnfimus, superlative form of īnferus (“low, deep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.
Borrowed from Latin īnflātiōnem. Cf. also enfiagione, which may be a doublet.
From giustific(are) (“to justify”) + -ato (1ˢᵗ conjugation past participle suffix).
Borrowed from Latin iniūstitia. By surface analysis, in- (“un-”, “not”) + giusto (“just, right”) + -izia (“-ice”, abstract noun-forming suffix).
From Latin iniūstus. By surface analysis, in- (“un-”, “not”) + giusto (“just”, “right”).
From Latin innātus (“inborn”), perfect active participle of innāscor (“be born in, grow up in”).
Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos).
From Latin innocuus (“harmless”). By surface analysis, in- (“not”, “un-”) + nocuo (“harmful”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin innovātiōnem.
From Latin inodōrus, with the ending reshaped by the influence of Italian odore (“smell”). By surface analysis, in- + odore.
Present participle of inquietare, influenced by French inquiétant, from Late Latin inquiētantem (“disturbing”), present active participle of inquiētō (“to disturb, disquiet”).
Borrowed from Late Latin īnsēnsātus. By surface analysis, in- + sensato.
From Latin īnsomnis, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From Latin īnsomnia, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
Borrowed from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem, from Latin īnspīrō. Doublet of ispirazione.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus.
Borrowed from French intermédiaire, from Latin intermedius.
Borrowed from German Allergie, coinage crafted using Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin invāsiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inventivus, from Latin inventum.
Borrowed from Latin investītūra. By surface analysis, investire + -tura.
Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiōnem (“unrolling, opening (a scroll)”, noun), derived from ēvolvō (“to unroll, unfold”).
From French hypnose, ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).
Inherited from Latin tempestās via the nominative form. Doublet of tempestà.
From Ancient Greek ὑποκρισίη (hupokrisíē), an uncommon form of ῠ̔πόκρῐσῐς (hŭpókrĭsĭs), from ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νομαι (hŭpokrī́nomai).
From Latin hypothēca (“pledge, mortgage”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”).
From neologia + -ico, or from French néologique.
Latinized form of archaic versions, from Latin nūtrīcem.
From vera (“true”, feminine singular) + -mente (“-ly”). Compare among others French vraiment.
Learned borrowing from New Latin Lītuānia.
Learned borrowing from Latin hīrtus (“hairy, shaggy”).
From Latin cōnfīdentem, present active participle of cōnfīdō.
From Medieval Latin dēsinentia (“ending”), from dēsinēre, from dēsinō (“to leave off, to end”). Compare French désinence.
From Latin īnsulānus, derived from īnsula (“island”).
Borrowed from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem, from Latin īnspīrō, or ispirare + -zione. Doublet of inspirazione.
From Medieval Latin īnstallāre (“to install, put in place, establish”), from in- + stallum (“stall”), from Frankish *stall (“stall, position, place”).
From Latin hystrīcem, from Ancient Greek ὕστριξ (hústrix). The porcupine exists in the wild in parts of southern Italy.
From Late Latin Iacobus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (yaʿăqōḇ, literally “he will/shall heel”), from עָקֵב (ʿāqēḇ, “heel”).
From igiene + -ico. Cognate with Piedmontese igiénich.
Borrowed from Latin hilaritātem, derived from hilaris (“cheerful”).
From Latin legālis. Compare the doublet leale.
Borrowed from Late Latin illūminātiōnem, from Latin illūminō.
From Latin illūstrātiōnem, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”). Cognate with Piedmontese ilustrassion.
From divorzio + -are; cognate with Piedmontese divorsié.

From paglia (“straw”) + -accio. Originally in sense 3 exclusively, sense 1 developed as the traditional Italian character's outfit was made of the same fabric used to cover straw mattresses. Cognate with Piedmontese pajasso.
From Medieval Latin astrolabium, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos, “star-taking”).
From Latin buxis (“box”), from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin imāginābilis.
From Latin corruptus, perfect passive participle of corrumpō (“to pervert; to taint”).
From Latin lepra, from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra, “leprosy”).
From Late Latin leprōsus. Doublet of leproso.
From Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).
From nebbia + -oso; first appears 13th century. Piecewise doublet of nebuloso, which is borrowed from Latin.
From Late Latin malefactōrem, from Latin malefaciō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin immanēns, immanentis, from Latin immanēre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin immersiōnem.

Derived regressively from the verb scalzare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *excalceus, itself either from a shortening of Latin excalceatus, or from ex- + calceus. Compare Neapolitan scauzo, Sicilian scausu, Corsican scalzu; cf. also Spanish descalzo, Portuguese descalço, Catalan descalç, French déchaux, Friulian discolç, Romanian desculț, Ladin deschëuz, from a related Vulgar Latin root.
Borrowed from Old French sentier, from Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita.
Latin armenus. The stress shifted due to analogy with Armenia.
From s- (“out of”) + bocca (“mouth”) + -are. Morphologically equivalent to French déboucher, though quite different in meaning.
From destro + -ezza. Compare Spanish and Portuguese destreza.
Borrowed from Latin immūtātus. By surface analysis, in- + mutato.
Borrowed from Old French gonfalon, from Frankish *gundfano, from Proto-Germanic *gunþifanô.
From Latin amphibius, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of the lips”), derived from Latin labium (“lip”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang loosely”).
From Ancient Greek λάρυγξ (lárunx), λάρυγγος (larungos, “larynx, throat”), of pre-Greek origin.
Borrowed from Latin lātitūdinem (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”). By surface analysis, lato + -itudine.
Borrowed from Old Occitan or Old French leial, from Latin legālis, whence also the doublet legale.
Borrowed from Latin glandem. Compare the inherited doublet ghianda.
From Latin imperītia (“inexperience; ignorance”). By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + perizia (“skill, ability”).
Borrowed from Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos).

Borrowed from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (“oneself”) and -cīdium (“-cide”). Up until the 19th century, the plural form was spelled suicidî, to distinguish it from the plural of suicida (“a suicidal person”).
Borrowed from Latin separātiōnem. By surface analysis, separare + -zione.
From Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma), from διαδέω (diadéō, “to bind around”).
From Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs).
From Medieval Latin residentia, from Latin residēns (“residing”), from resideō (“to reside”), from re- + sedeō (“to sit”).
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “I flow”).
From Ancient Greek διχότομος (dikhótomos, “equally divided, cut in half”).
Borrowed from Latin explōsiōnem, derived from to eject” ← “to drive out by clapping.
From de- (“de-, un-”) + cespuglio (“bush”) + -tore (“-er”, agent noun suffix).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek διδασκαλία (didaskalía, “instruction”), from διδάσκαλος (didáskalos, “teacher”).
From Latin diffāmātiōnem. Cognate with Piedmontese difamassion.
From earlier priscione, possibly via Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiōnem (“the act of seizing”), from prehendō (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of prensione.

From Latin carcerem, from Proto-Italic *karkros, from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”), in the sense of “enclosure”. Cognate to Old Catalan càrcer/carçre, Spanish cárcel and Portuguese cárcere.
Derived from Vulgar Latin certificāre, from Latin certus (“resolved, certain”), a modified form of the perfect passive participle of cernō.
From Latin cērōtum (“wax plaster”), ultimately from Ancient Greek κηρός (kērós, “beeswax”). Cognate with Piedmontese siròt.
Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin and Late Latin sacrāmentum, from Latin sacrō.
From fidelizza(re) (“to loyalize”) + -zione (“-(a)tion”), on the example of French fidélisation.
Inherited from Latin macellārius. By surface analysis, macello + aio. Compare Romanian măcelar.
Borrowed from Late Latin statiōnārius, from statiō, statiōnis.
From Latin spectrum (“apparition, specter”), derived from speciō (“to look at, behold”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alterūi, corresponding to Classical Latin alterī (dative singular of alter). The -ui ending, analogous to lui, colui, costui, cotestui, codestui, is ultimately due to the influence of Latin cui. Compare French autrui.
From Vulgar Latin *sūgillum, from Latin sigillum. Doublet of sigillo.
Borrowed from French mangouste, from Portuguese mangusto, from Marathi मुंगूस (muṅgūs).
From Latin simulātiōnem. By surface analysis, simulare + -zione.
Borrowed from Latin accelerātiōnem (“hastening; acceleration”). By surface analysis, accelerare (“to accelerate”) + -zione.
From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis).
Borrowed from French analyser. By surface analysis, analisi + -izzare.
From Ancient Greek παθολογικός (pathologikós). Compare French pathologique.
From cotica (“pork rind”) + -ino (diminutive suffix). The -e- is due to dialectal influence.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin receptiōnem (“the act of receiving; reception”), from recipiō (“receive”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to hold”), or from ricevere + -zione. Doublet of recezione.
From arci- + vescovo; modeled on Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “first, chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).
Borrowed from French comptable, from compter. By surface analysis, contare + -abile.
From Latin scandalum. Cognate with Sicilian scànnalu.
Borrowed from Latin iūdiciārius. By surface analysis, giudizio (“judgement”) + -ario (“-ary”, “pertaining to”).
Borrowed from Latin iūdiciālis. By surface analysis, giudizio (“judgement”) + -ale (“-al”, “pertaining to”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin competentia.
From udire + -enza, a calque of Latin audientia.
From Latin macellum, related to Ancient Greek μάκελλον (mákellon), μάκελλος (mákellos).
From New Latin praelīmināris. Cognate to French préliminaire.
Borrowed from Latin incandēscentem, present active participle of incandēscō (“to grow warm; to kindle”).
Back-formation from testimonî, plural of testimonio (“testimony; witness”), perceived as testimoni.
Borrowed from Late Latin abstentiōnem, from Latin abstentus, from abstineō.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin resultāre, from resiliō.
From alto- + parlante, a calque of English loudspeaker modelled on French haut-parleur.
Borrowed from Latin impugnātiōnem (“attack, assault”), derived from impugnō (“to attack, to fight against”).
From Latin subscrīptiōnem, influenced by sottoscrivere.
From Latin aegida, from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́ς (aigĭ́s).
From Late Latin exorcizāre, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζειν (exorkízein, “banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”).
Borrowed from Latin violātiōnem (“injury, profanation”), from violō (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”).
From French montgolfière, from the name of the Montgolfier brothers, inventors of the hot-air balloon.
From Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “insertion”).
From Late Latin urgentia. Cognate with Piedmontese urgensa/ürgensa.
From Late Latin planētārius (“astrologer, relating to the planets”), from Latin planēta (“planet, wandering star”).
Probably borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).
From trattare + -mento; Cognate with Piedmontese tratament.
Borrowed from Latin onus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃énh₂os, from the root *h₃enh₂- (“to onerate, charge”).
From Latin laetāmen (“dung, manure”) < laetus (“happy, rich”, also later “fertile”). Compare Dalmatian lotum.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnfectiōnem (“making, preparing, producing, arranging, composing, completing”).
Borrowed from French autoriser, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre. Doublet of ottriare.
Borrowed from French étiquette. Doublet of ticket.
From gradire + -evole. Compare Catalan and Spanish agradable, French agréable and Portuguese agradável. Doublet of aggradevole.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obiectīvus.
From Latin polygamus, from Ancient Greek πολύγαμος (polúgamos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek αἱματικός (haimatikós), from αἷμᾰ, αἵμᾰτος (haîmă, haímătos, “blood”).
Borrowed from French madame or Calque of French madame. Sense two derives from the fact that during the mid-19ᵗʰ century, the main police headquarters in Turin were seated in Palazzo Madama.
From Latin comprēnsus, variant of comprehensus.
From Latin ingredientem (“entering”), from ingredior (“to enter”).
From impegnare + -ivo. Cognate with Piedmontese impegnativ.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin potentiālis.

Borrowed from French bistouri, in turn from archaic Italian pistorese or pistorino (“from Pistoia”, see Latin Pistōrium); the city of Pistoia was once famous for the manufacturing of blades. Doublet of pistoiese.
From earlier ruina, from Latin ruīna.
Borrowed from Latin hospitālis, whence also Italian ospedale (an inherited doublet) and hotel (through French).
From Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia).
From cane (“dog”) + -lino (diminutive suffix), using the root found in cagna (“female dog”).
Borrowed from French terrasse, from Old Occitan terrassa. Related to terrazzo.
From Latin fūmantem, present participle of fūmō.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin trānsfōrmātiōnem, from Latin trānsfōrmō. By surface analysis, tras- + formazione.
Ultimately from Latin dimissio with a reintroduced epenthetic -s-, possibly influenced by English dismiss. Doublet of dimissione. Compare dimettere.
From Late Latin cammīnus, from Gaulish. Cognate with Sicilian caminu (“walk, way / chimney”), which never geminated.
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmicrānia, from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă). Doublet of micragna.
From Latin beneficiārius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”).
From Medieval Latin manutentiōnem, form of manutentiō, derived from Latin manū tenēre.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin priōritātem.
From Late Latin mundānus. Compare French mondain.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin entitātem.
Borrowed from Latin capitulum. Doublet of capecchio, which is the inherited form.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin capitulāre (“draw up under headings”), from Latin capitulum (“heading, chapter, title”), diminutive of caput (“head”).
Borrowed from French accise, itself from Old French acceis (“tax”).
From Latin brachia, bracchia, plural of bracchium. Compare Portuguese braça, Spanish braza, Old French brace.
Borrowed from French majoritaire, from majorité.
From Latin mānsiōnem, either inherited or borrowed from Old French maison.
From Late Latin trophaeum, variant of Latin tropaeum (“trophy, victory memorial”), from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turning, trope”), from τρέπω (trépō, “to turn”).
From garbo (“politeness”) + -ato. Cognate with Piedmontese garbà.
Borrowed from Late Latin territōriālis, from Latin territōrium. By surface analysis, territorio + -ale.
Borrowed from Latin prōductōrem, from Latin prōductus.
From Latin picem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pī́ts (“pitch; resin”).
Probably borrowed from Latin mēnsa (“table”), although some sources disagree.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρόμβος (thrómbos, “clot, curd”).
From Late Latin rēnālis, from Latin rēn.
From andro- + -logo, on the model of ginecologo (“gynecologist”).
From Latin pāgānus (“rural; villager”), derived from pāgus (“area outside of a city; countryside”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin crēdibilitātem, from Latin credibilis.
From valente, or Late Latin valentia, from Latin valēns.
Learned borrowing from Latin feretrum, from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron).
From Ancient Greek μῆνιγξ (mêninx, “skin, membrane; lees of wine”).
From lavare + -aggio. Compare French lavage, Spanish lavaje, Portuguese lavagem, Catalan llavatge.
From a- + cieco + -are, from Latin caecus.
Borrowed from Latin nōmenclātūra (“a calling by name, list of names”). Doublet of nomenklatura.
From abbreviare, itself a borrowing from Latin abbreviāre (“to abbreviate, to shorten”). Doublet of abregé, borrowed from French.
Borrowed from Latin mediānus, whence also mezzano (an inherited doublet).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin applicābilis.
Inherited from Latin reversus, with progressive rs→sː→ʃː assimilation (compare vescica and ganascia). Doublet of riverso. Cognate with Sicilian riversu.
Borrowed from Latin magnitūdinem. Doublet of magnitudo.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin magnitūdinem. Doublet of magnitudine.
From ormone + -ale, on the model of English hormonal.
From Late Latin ūnificāre. Cognate with Piedmontese unifiché/ünifiché.
From finale + -izzare. Meaning "to finalize" is a calque of English finalize.
Uncertain if inherited or semi-borrowed from Latin magnus, from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, derived from *méǵh₂s (“big; great”).
Borrowed from Late Latin chartāceus. By surface analysis, carta + -aceo.
From giovine (“young”) + -ezza (“-ness”, suffix denoting a state of being). Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *juvenitia. Compare French jeunesse.
Inherited from Old Italian gioventude, gioventute, from Latin iuventūtem.
Borrowed from French aviateur, ultimately from Latin avis (“bird”).
From Latin asylum, from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).
From earlier catastro, a borrowing from Venetan catastico, from Medieval Greek κατάστιχον (katástikhon, “line by line”).
Borrowed from French climatique, from Ancient Greek κλιματικός (klimatikós), from κλῐ́μᾰ, κλῐ́μᾰτος (klĭ́mă, klĭ́mătos). By surface analysis, clima + -ico.
From Ancient Greek εὐφορία (euphoría), from εὔφορος (eúphoros) "bearing well".
From Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”).
Borrowed from French margarine (“margarine”), from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs, “pearl”).
Borrowed from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of beton.
Borrowed from Latin circumscrīptiōnem (“outline”). Compare French circonscription (“electoral district”).
From Ancient Greek αὐτόνομος (autónomos). By surface analysis, auto- + -nomo.
From Ancient Greek μαιευτικός (maieutikós, “obstetric”). Compare English maieutics.
From Ancient Greek μαιευτικός (maieutikós, “obstetric”). Compare English maieutic.
From Latin orgia, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia).
From Medieval Latin and Late Latin notōrius.
Inherited from Latin falcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelk-, *dʰelg- (“a cutting tool”). Compare French faux.
Borrowed from French glace. Doublet of ghiaccia.
Named after Perpetua, Don Abbondio's gossipy servant from Alessandro Manzoni's The Betrothed.
Borrowed from Latin corruptiōnem, derived from corruptus, perfect passive participle of corrumpō (“to pervert; to taint”).
From leggero + -ezza; cognate with Piedmontese legerëssa.
From Hebrew מַלְאָכִי (mal'achi, malʼāḵî, literally “my messenger”).
Borrowed from Late Latin passionālis, from passiō; by surface analysis, passione + -ale.
Inherited from Latin campānella. By surface analysis, campana + -ella.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin metaphysica, from Ancient Greek μετὰ τὰ φυσικά (metà tà phusiká, literally “after that which is natural”).

Borrowed from Latin aevum, from earlier aevom, from Old Latin aivom, from Proto-Italic *aiwom (“period”, “age”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂óyu (“long time”, “lifetime”), from the root *h₂ey- (“vital force”, “life”, “age”, “eternity”).
Borrowed from Latin pāpātus. By surface analysis, papa + -ato.
Borrowed from Latin ōtium (“leisure”). Compare Portuguese ócio, Spanish ocio.
Borrowed from English psychedelic, derived from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “mind, soul”) + δῆλος (dêlos, “manifest, visible”).
From Latin platea + -ale. See also Italian platea.
From Latin meditātiōne(m), case form of meditātiō (“thinking, contemplation”). By surface analysis, medita(re) (“to meditate”) + -zione (“-ation”).
Borrowed from French débuter (“to lead off”).
Derived from Late Latin melodicus, from Greek μελωδικός (melodikós). By surface analysis, melodia + -ico.
From diverso + -ficare; cognate with Piedmontese diversifiché.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin intitulāre.
Borrowed from Latin operātōrem. By surface analysis, operare + -tore.
From federal(e) (“federal”) + -ista (“-ist”), on the example of French fédéraliste.
From Latin naufragium, compound of navis (“ship”) and the root of the verb frangō (“to break”).
From sovra, modeled after Old French soverain, Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super, whence also soprano. Cognate to French souverain, Spanish and Portuguese soberano. Doublet of soprano.
Borrowed from Old Occitan trabucar, ultimately from Frankish *būk; with influence from Italian bocca.
Borrowed from Old French traïner, from Vulgar Latin *tragināre, from *tragere, from Latin trahere (“to drag”) (compare trarre). Doublet of trascinare, which was inherited.
From English photogenic and French photogénique. By surface analysis, foto- + -genico.
From Old French travailler, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device”).
From Late Latin coetāneus, coaetāneus, derived from Classical Latin aetās (“age”).
From Latin nāvālis, derived from nāvis (“boat”).
From trattare (“to treat”) + -iva. Compare Piedmontese tratativa.
Borrowed from Latin contrādictiōnem. By surface analysis, contra- + dizione.
From Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin hēreticus, haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”).
From rapire + -mento; cognate with Piedmontese rapiment.
From Old Occitan savi, from Vulgar Latin *sapium (“wise”), from Latin sapidus (“delicious, wise”). Doublet of sapido, a borrowing from Latin.
Borrowed from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”).
Learned borrowing from Latin dignitātem. Doublet of degnità.
From Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin superiōritātem, derived from Latin superior. By surface analysis, superiore + -ità.
Borrowed from Late Latin tribulātiōnem, from Latin tribulō.
From malo + anno. Cognate with Piedmontese malann.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frontālis, from Latin frontem.
From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diametrālis. By surface analysis, diametro (“diameter”) + -ale.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abstractiōnem.
Borrowed from French phonétique, from Ancient Greek φωνητικός (phōnētikós).
From Latin rigorōsus. By surface analysis, rigore + -oso.
Calque of English contraceptive, from contra- + -cettivo.
Inherited from Latin maltha, from Ancient Greek μάλθα (máltha).
Borrowed from Latin episcopālis (“of or pertaining to a bishop”). Compare vescovo.
From Late Latin dēstrūctīvus, from the past participle of Latin dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus. By surface analysis, distrutto + -ivo.
Borrowed from Latin dēstrūctiōnem. By surface analysis, distruggere + -zione.
From Late Latin sapōrōsus, from Latin sapor.
From gusto + -oso. Cognate with Piedmontese gustos.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin āctuālitātem, derived from Late Latin āctuālis, derived from Latin āctus.
From Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ (hárpuiă, literally “snatcher”).
From Latin ēlūsus + -ivo, from the perfect passive participle of ēlūdō (“to deceive, to escape”).
From ciclo + motore, on the model of French cyclomoteur.
From Latin vilipendere, from vilis (“base, cheap”) and pendere (“to consider”).
Borrowed from French allier, itself from Latin alligāre. Doublet of the inherited allegare.
From so- (attenuating prefix) + chiudere (“to close, shut”).
From Late Latin intingere, from Latin tingō.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós, “bellicose, hostile”), from πόλεμος (pólemos, “war, battle”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολεμίζω (polemízō, “I fight”), derived from πόλεμος (pólemos, “fight”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *falciāre (compare French faucher), from Latin falx (“sickle, scythe”), from Proto-Indo-European *dhalk-, *dhalg- (“a cutting tool”).
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin sculptūra (“act of carving; sculpture”), derived from sculpō (“to carve”) + -tūra (“-ing, -ure”, action noun suffix).
From Late Latin foederātiōnem (“federation, treaty”), derived from Latin foederō (“to sign a treaty or agreement”), derived from foedus (“pact, agreement”).
Borrowed from French support, from the verb supporter, ultimately from Latin supportāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin corrōsiō, corrōsiōnem (“gnawing away, corroding”), from Latin corrōdō (“gnaw away, corrode”).
From vincere + -tore. Compare French vainqueur, Spanish and Portuguese vencedor.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (al-malḡam, “emollient poultice or unguent for sores”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient”), from μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”), from μαλακός (malakós, “soft”).
Borrowed from English ion, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión).
From reagire + -tore, on the model of agire/attore.
Internationalism, first attested as English electron. By surface analysis, elettro- + -one.
From saldare + -tura; cognate with Piedmontese saldadura.
Internationalism, first attested as English proton. By surface analysis, proto- + -one.
From Ancient Greek ἐνθάλπω (enthálpō), from θάλπω (thálpō).
From in- + coraggio (“courage”) + -are. Compare Old French encoragier for an analogous construction.
Borrowed from Late Latin prōvocātiōnem (“challenge”, “provocation”), from Latin prōvocō. By surface analysis, provocare (“to provoke”) + -zione (“-tion”).
From ri- + lasciare. For the sense “relax,” likely a semantic loan from Latin relaxō.
From Latin penetrātiōnem. By surface analysis, penetrare + -zione.
From Late Latin *malia, from Latin malus. Cognate with Sicilian magghiardu.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin excitābilis.
Borrowed from Old French joieus. By surface analysis, gioia + -oso.
Borrowed from Latin odiōsus, derived from odium (“hatred”).
From Late Latin terminālis, from Latin terminus.
Evolution of Latin ōscillāri, ōscillātus, ōscillātiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin sequentia, from Latin sequēns.
From Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”).
Borrowed from Late Latin discrētiōnem, from Latin discernō.

Borrowed from French garçon, from Old French garçon, from Medieval Latin garciō, from earlier *warciō, from Frankish *wrakkijō (“mercenary; servant”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile; warrior”). Cognate with Sicilian jarzuni.
Inherited from Latin ducātus. See also the doublets dogado and dogato.
Borrowed from Latin grātus (whence also grado, an inherited doublet), from Proto-Italic *gʷrātos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥Htós, derived from the root *gʷerH- (“to praise; to elevate”).
Unadapted borrowing from English Wikipedia, blend of Hawaiian wiki (“speedy”) + English encyclopedia. By surface analysis, Hawaiian wiki + -pedia (“-pedia”).
Borrowed from Latin excelsus, from excellō (“to elevate”).
From in- + sapone (“soap”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From fritto + -ura, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīctus. Compare French friture, Romanian friptură, Spanish and Portuguese fritura, Sicilian frittura.
From Latin amiantus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μῐ́ᾰντος (ămĭ́ăntos).
From s- + gradevole. Compare Catalan and Spanish desagradable, French désagréable and Portuguese desagradável.
From Latin trānscendere. By surface analysis, tra- + scendere.
From Latin scindere, from Proto-Italic *skindō, from Proto-Indo-European *skinédti (“to be cutting off”), derived from the root *skeyd- (“to split”).
Borrowed from Latin argenteus. By surface analysis, argento (“silver”) + -eo (“-ous”).
Borrowed from Latin malitiōsus. By surface analysis, malizia (“malice”) + -oso.

From Latin parasītus, from Ancient Greek παράσῑτος (parásītos, “person who eats at the table of another”). Ending reshaped by erroneous analogy with the suffix -ita, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).
Borrowed from French détailler, from Old French detaillier.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”). By surface analysis, proietto + -ile.
Calque of French interférer. By surface analysis, inter- + ferire.
From Late Latin praefixum, from Latin praefixus.
From Latin revēlātōrem. By surface analysis, rivelare + -tore.
Diminutive of Latin lancea. Compare with Piedmontese lansëtta.
From a- + nero + -ire. Cf. also Latin nigrēscō, French noircir, Spanish ennegrecer, Romanian înnegri.
Borrowed from Latin ēvolventem (“unrolling”), present active participle of ēvolvō (“to unroll, unwind”).
Borrowed from Latin pigmentum. Doublet of pimento.
From Latin igneus. By surface analysis, igne (“fire”) + -eo (“-ous”).
Borrowed from Latin diffringere; re-formed by analogy with frangere.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin calamina, q.v.
From Latin (lapis) haematites, from Ancient Greek αἱματίτης λίθος (haimatítēs líthos, “hematite”, literally “blood-red stone”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).
From indurare with change of conjugation, from Latin indūrāre.
Borrowed from Latin prōscrībere (“to advertise, proclaim; to publish; to proscribe, ban; to outlaw, banish”), from prō + scrībō (“to write”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem (with later change of declension), accusative of Latin *scrība, from Latin scrība (“writer, scribe”), with altered declension. Compare Occitan escrivan, French écrivain, Spanish escribano. Doublet of scriba.
From Latin absorptus, perfect passive participle of absorbeō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin fīlāmentum, from Late Latin fīlō (“to spin, draw out in a long line”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
From Late Latin mufrō (“wild sheep”), related to Latin musimō (“wild sheep”), both probably of pre-Roman substrate origin.
Borrowed from Latin Iūlius. Doublet of luglio.
From Old French bersail (“target for an arrow”), from berser (“to hunt with bow and arrow”), from Latin vervēx (“wether, kind of goat; blockhead, idiot”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin exigentia.
Borrowed from French assoupir, re-Latinized from Old French assouvir, from Vulgar Latin *assōpīre, from Latin sōpīre (“to put to sleep”).
From in- + veleno + -ire. Akin to English envenom, French envenimer, French envenenar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *massīcius, from Latin massa. By surface analysis, massa + -iccio.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin armistitium, from Latin arma (“weapons”) and statio (“immobility”) (compare solstitium). Cognate to French and English armistice; Galician and Spanish armisticio; Portuguese armistício; Catalan armistici.
Borrowed from Latin laurus. Doublet of the inherited alloro.
Learned borrowing from Latin līberātiōnem (“liberation, release”).
From Ancient Greek στρατηγικός (stratēgikós). By surface analysis, strategia + -ico.
From Medieval Latin faida, borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“enmity; feud”).
From cancello + -iere, or from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancellus. Cognate with Sicilian canciḍḍeri.
From Latin decennālis (“decennial”), from decennis (“10-year”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”).
From Ancient Greek ἱεραρχικός (hierarkhikós). By surface analysis, gerarchia + -ico.
From stra- + potere. First attested in 1848.
Past participle of benedire, from Ecclesiastical Latin benedictus, from Latin benedīcō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōtocollum, from Medieval Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratificāre, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”) + faciō (“to make”).
From Old Occitan frontiera, from front. Compare French frontière.
From dis- + pari; cognate with Piedmontese dìspar. Compare Sicilian sparu~spariggiu.
Unadapted borrowing from Late Latin laudanum (“opium tincture, laudanum”)
Inherited from Latin crāticius, from crātis.
Inherited from Latin (oc)cāsiōnem with apheresis. Doublet of occasione, a borrowing from Latin. Compare Sicilian scaciuni.
From Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).

From earlier mariscalco, from Medieval Latin mariscalcus, itself from Frankish *marhaskalk (“servant assigned to horses”), from *marh + *skalk, whence also French maréchal, English marshal, Spanish mariscal. Doublet of maresciallo.
From Late Latin coemeterium, Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion).
From Latin opus, cognate with Old Spanish uebos, Romanian op.
Borrowed from Late Latin balneāris, from Latin balneum.
From Latin mīlitia. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from Polish milicja.
Latinized form of older giudio, from Latin iūdaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Hebrew יהודי (Yehudi).
From grato + -itudine; cognate with Piedmontese gratitùdin.
From grano + -aio or from Latin grānārium.
Back-formation from inquisito, from Latin inquīsītus, perfect passive participle of inquīrō (“to investigate”).

From torrente, from Latin torrentem, present active participle of torreō (“to scorch, burn, parch”), from Proto-Italic *torzeō, causative of the Proto-Indo-European root *ters- (“dry”). By surface analysis, torrent(e) (“torrent”, “stream”) + -izio (derivational suffix).
Inherited from Latin frumentum, from fruor (“to enjoy”).
Haplology from Late Latin īdōlolatrēs, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολᾰ́τρης (eidōlolắtrēs).
Formed from sopra- + ciglio, based on Latin supercilium.
From Latin pēnsilis (“hanging”). Doublet of pesolo. Compare Portuguese pênsil.
From Latin prioratus. By surface analysis, priore + -ato.
Borrowed from French hasard, from Old French hasart, from Arabic اَلزَّهْر (az-zahr, “the dice”). Doublet of zara.
From arpione + -are, from a variant of arpone (“harpoon”).
From ondulare + -zione; cf. Medieval or New Latin undulatio.
From Latin praedātōrem. By surface analysis, predare + -tore.

From Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía, “rule of a high priest”), from ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”) (compare -archia).
From Latin cōnfīdentia. By surface analysis, confid(ente) + -enza.
From Latin possessivus (“possessive”), from possideō (“to possess”), from potis (“able”) + sedeō (“sit”).
Deverbal from soffiare + -o. Compare Sicilian çuççu.
Borrowed from Latin oestrus, from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros, “vehement desire, frenzy”, literally “gadfly”).
From Latin olfactus, derived from olfaciō (“to smell, scent”).
Borrowed from Latin antonomasia, from Ancient Greek ἀντονομασία (antonomasía, “antonomasia”).
From occorrere + -enza. Cf. Medieval Latin occurrentia.
From Latin corporeus. By surface analysis, corpor- (“body”, fossilized stem for corpo) + -eo.
Borrowed from Latin nūtrientem, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).
From scenografia + -ico, equivalent to Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ) + γρᾰφή (grăphḗ) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin saeculāris. The meanings related to religion started developing through the works of Christian authors.
From specchio (“mirror”) + -are. Cf. also Latin speculārī.

Borrowed from Old Occitan salvatge, from Vulgar Latin *salvāticus, from Latin silvāticus (“of the woods”). Doublet of the inherited selvatico. Compare Sicilian sarbaggiu, Spanish salvaje, Portuguese selvagem, Catalan salvatge, Piedmontese salvaj.
The sense referring to a style of art and music is borrowed from French baroque.
Deverbal from varcare + -o. Cognate with Friulian varc, Piedmontese varch.
Borrowed from Latin reversus. Doublet of rovescio.
From Latin quercea, nominalized feminine form of the adjective querceus (“oaken, of oak”), derived from quercus (“oak”). Compare Neapolitan and Sicilian cerza.
Probably borrowed from Latin ligneus. By surface analysis, lign- (“wood”, fossilized stem for legno) + -eo.
From Late Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek πᾰρένθεσῐς (părénthesĭs).
From anno + -ata, or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annāre; compare French année.
Borrowed from French châle, from Hindi शाल (śāl), from Classical Persian شال (šāl).

From ubriaco (“drunk”) + -are, from Late Latin ēbriācus, derived from Latin ēbrius, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”). By surface analysis, ubriac(o) (“drunk”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix).
From Ancient Greek ἀγρονόμος (agronómos). By surface analysis, agro- + -nomo.
From Latin arātrum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
From Late Latin arātūra, from Latin arō. Compare Spanish aradura, Romanian arătură.
Inherited from Latin sēminātōrem. Morphologically, seminare + -tore.
From Latin trivium, derived from tri- (“three”) + via (“road”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἑλικοειδής (helikoeidḗs, “spiral”, adjective), derived from ἕλιξ (hélix, “spiral”, noun).
From Latin sulcus, from Proto-Indo-European *solk-o- (“furrow”), *selk- (“to pull, drag”).
Borrowed from Late Latin extēnsīvus, from Latin extēnsus.
Latinization of earlier vetrano, inherited from Latin veterānus; partly borrowed in military/experience senses.
Of northern Italian origin, from Late Latin mediator (via the nominative), from Latin medius. Cf. also French métayer, Spanish mediero, Sicilian mitateri. Doublet of mediatore.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus.
From Latin sequāx (“following”). Cognate with Spanish secuaz and Portuguese sequaz.
Borrowed from Latin praedātiōnem. By surface analysis, predare + -zione.
From the Latin navicella, from navis.
From aero- + -dina, on the model of English aerodyne.
From aero- + statica, on the model of French aérostatique.
Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō.
From Latin prunus, from Ancient Greek.
From Latin silurus, borrowed from Ancient Greek σίλουρος (sílouros).
Borrowed from French mitrailler, or mitraglia + -are.
Borrowed from Old Occitan lauzenga, from Frankish *lausungu.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōpulsiōnem, from Latin propulsus.
From Late Latin fūnerālis (“pertaining to a funeral”), from Latin funus.
Borrowed from French jury, from English jury. Same etymon as giurì.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *serpes, from Latin serpēns, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-.
Borrowed from French fourgon. Cognate with Piedmontese furgon.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin licentiāre. Compare French licencier.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin assaltus, derived from assaliō, from Latin assiliō (“to rush at”).
Borrowed from Spanish bellaco (“scoundrel”), under influence from vile. Compare Portuguese velhaco.
From Late Latin cabanna, capanna (see further etymology there). Compare Spanish cabaña.
From a- (“to”) + giusto (“just”, “right”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From Catalan barraca, probably from Paleo-Hispanic. Compare also barocco.
From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).
Borrowed from Old French blasmer. Doublet of bestemmiare and blasfemare. Cognate with Sicilian jastimijari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carōnia, from Latin carō (“flesh, meat”). Compare French charogne.
Borrowed from Latin cautiōnem (“precaution, caution”), derived from caveō (“to beware, avoid”).
From Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “bile”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin compassiōnem, from Latin compatior.
Borrowed from French complot, from Middle French complot.
From tranquillo + -izzare, on the example of French tranquilliser.
From Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum. Doublet of the borrowed dorso.

From Latin aetherem (“the upper pure, bright air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “upper air”), from αἴθω (aíthō, “to burn, shine”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂eydʰ- (“to ignite, burn”).
From Latin geniālis (“of or pertaining to marriage; festive, genial”), from genius (“guardian spirit”) + -ālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūstificātiōnem, from iūstificō, from Latin iūstus.
Borrowed from French engager. By surface analysis, in- + gaggio (“wage”, “salary”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix).
From Latin ligna, plural of lignum, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-no- (“that which is collected”), from *leǵ-.
From Latin mantēllum (“covering, cloak”), diminutive of mantum, probably from Gaulish. Compare French manteau.
From Latin mūtandae, from mūtandus (“which is to be changed”).
Borrowed from Old French homage, from Medieval Latin homināticum, from homo (“man”).
From Latin Orcus (“god of the underworld”), orcus.
From Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from a Medieval Greek *ἀπόδειξα (*apódeixa), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof”). Doublet of the learned borrowing apodissi.
From rapina + -are; cognate with Piedmontese rapiné.
Borrowed from Latin ratiōnem. Doublet of ragione (inherited).
Borrowed from Latin rixa. Doublet of ressa, which was inherited.
From Late Latin sympathīa, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).
From Latin satisfactiōnem (“reparation, amends”). By surface analysis, soddisfa(re) (“to satisfy”) + -zione (“-tion”, noun-forming suffix).
Borrowed from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spiritus.
Borrowed from Old French torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, from torqua, from Latin torquēs, torquīs (“wreath”), from torqueō (“twist”, verb).
Borrowed from French wagon, from English wagon, itself from Dutch wagen.
From Late Latin vindicātōrem, from Latin vindicō.
From Latin affirmātīvus. By surface analysis, affermare + -ivo.
From a- + lungo + -are or from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre (cf. also elongāre), from Latin longus. Compare French allonger.
Borrowed from Old French archier. By surface analysis, arco + -iere.
From azzardo + -are. Akin to French hasarder.
From Vulgar Latin *serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“to fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”).
From bocca (“mouth”) + -ata. Compare Vulgar Latin *buccata, French bouchée, Romanian bucată, Portuguese bocado, and Spanish bocado.
From brigare (“to form a troop, fight”) + -ata.
Borrowed from Spanish camarada (“comrade”), from cámara (“chamber”) derived from Latin camera (“chamber”).
From an older castore, from Latin castōrem, from Ancient Greek Κάστωρ (Kástōr).
Learned borrowing from Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”).
From Old French congiet, from commeātus (whence also Italian commiato).
Borrowed from Latin convictiōnem. By surface analysis, convincere + -zione.
Borrowed from Latin cordiālis. Noun meaning via French.
From difetto + -oso; Cognate with Piedmontese difetos.
From Late Latin dēsertōrem, from Latin dēsertus.
From dis- + ubbidire (“to obey”). Cognate with Piedmontese disubidì, French désobéir.

Learned borrowing from New Latin elasticus (“elastic”), from Ancient Greek as if *ἐλαστής (*elastḗs) for ἐλατής (elatḗs), equiv. to ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “a driver, hurler”), from ἐλαύνειν (elaúnein, “to drive, set in motion, push, strike, beat out”). Cognate with Piedmontese elàstich.
From Latin emporium (“market”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπορεῖον (emporeîon), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “marketer”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πόρος (póros, “travel”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).
From Latin evāsus, passive participle of evadĕre (“to elude, escape”) + -ivo.
Borrowed from French farce. Doublet of farcia.
From Latin flagellāre, probably borrowed or latinized.
From Late Latin fossātum, from Latin fossō (“dig”).
Inherited from Latin fūnem. Compare Romanian funie.
Borrowed from Latin gelidus, derived from gelū, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *gel- (“cold”).
Borrowed from Old French jergon, jargon.
Borrowed from Old French joste, derived from joster.
Inherited from Old Italian giovenile, from Latin iuvenīlem, derived from iuvenis (“young”). By surface analysis, giovane (“young”, noun) + -ile (“-ile; tending to”).
From grano (“grain”) + -ello; cognate with Piedmontese granel.
From Latin gregem. Cognate with Galician grea, Portuguese grei, Spanish grey.
Derived from guarire (“to heal; to recover”) + -gione (“-(a)tion”, action noun suffix), on the example of Old French garison. Cognate with Ligurian goarixon, Piedmontese guarigion.
From in- + catenare, possibly also corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *incatēnāre, from Latin catēnāre. Compare French enchaîner, Spanish and Occitan encadenar, Portuguese encadear, Friulian incjadenâ.
From in- + chiodo (“nail”) + -are. Compare inchiudere and includere. Cognate with Sicilian nchiuvari.
From in- + ciampa + -are, older variant of zampa (“paw”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin indūmentum (“garment”).
From in- + ginocchio + -are + -si. Compare French agenouiller, Catalan agenollar, Portuguese ajoelhar, Romanian îngenunchea.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lasso and lazo.
From Vulgar Latin *luciniōlum < *lucinium, alteration of Late Latin licinium (influenced by lūx (“light”)), from ellychnium, from Ancient Greek. Compare French lumignon.
Borrowed from Old French mastin, from Vulgar Latin *mans'tinus < *mansuetīnus (“tamed (animal)”), from Latin mānsuetus (“tamed”).
Older form of maestro, from Latin magistrum.
From signore under influence from Middle French monseigneur.
Borrowed from Spanish mezquita, from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, “place of worship”).
Learned borrowing from Latin nātālicius (“birth, birthday”).
From oltre- + passare. Compare passare oltre. Compare also French outrepasser and passer outre.
Borrowed from Old French honte, from Early Medieval Latin haunta, borrowed from Frankish *haunitha, from Proto-Germanic *hauniþō (“humiliation”).
Inherited from Latin aurificem. Doublet of orafo.
From Latin hostīlis, derived from hostis (“enemy”).
From Mediaeval Greek παρακονη (parakonē, "whetstone"), from Ancient Greek παρακονάω (parakonáō, “I sharpen, whet”), from παρά (pará) + ἀκόνη (akónē, “whetstone”). Compare English paragon.
Borrowed from French parcelle, from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula. Doublet of particella and particola.
From Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).
Borrowed from Late Latin perquīsitiōnem, from Latin perquīrō.
From pietà + -oso; cognate with Friulian pietôs, Piedmontese pietos.
From presenti(re) (“to have a presentiment of”) + -mento (nominal derivational suffix). By surface analysis, pre- (“before”) + sentimento (“sentiment”, “sensation”).
From Old French profit, from Latin profectus.
From Late Latin rancōrem (“grudge” ← “rancidity”), from Latin ranceō (“to be rotten, putrid”).
Borrowed from Old French reame, reaume (whence also Modern French royaume).
Borrowed from French relais. Doublet of relais.
Borrowed from German Föhn, from Vulgar Latin *faōnius, from Latin Favōnius (“Favonius”), a Roman wind god.
From the nominative of Late Latin sartor, an agent noun based on Classical Latin sarcīre (“to darn”).
Inherited from Latin exāmen. Compare the borrowed doublet esame.
Borrowed from French écharpe, from Old French escharpe, from Frankish *skirpa (“bandoleer”), of either Germanic or Latin origin.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēdātivus, from Latin sēdātus, perfect passive participle of sēdō.

Inherited from Late Latin segusius (compare Portuguese sabujo, Spanish sabueso), from a Celtic language, from Proto-Celtic *sekʷetor (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor (“to follow”) (compare Irish seach).
From sereno (“clear, calm”), from Latin serenus (“calm”) or from the feminine past participle of serenare.
From Late Latin servītōrem, from Latin serviō.
Borrowed from Latin silentem, present active participle of sileō (“to be silent”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek συντονία (suntonía). Compare French syntonie and Portuguese sintonia.
Borrowed from Latin siparium, from Ancient Greek σίπαρος (síparos).
From Latin sōbrius (“sober”), from se- (“without”) + ēbrius (“intoxicated”).
From sotterra + -are, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *subterrāre, from Latin sub- + terra.
From Latin spurcitia. Internally, from sporco (“dirty”) + -izia.
From Latin squālidus (“dirty, foul”), derived from squāleō (“to be unkempt, neglected”).
From tenero + -ezza. Compare Catalan tendresa, Aromanian tinireatsã, Old Sicilian tinirizza, French tendresse, Romanian tinerețe, Spanish and Portuguese terneza.
From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos).
From Latin īnferus (“low”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.
Borrowed from Latin thōrax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax).
Deverbal from tragittare + -o. Cognate with Piedmontese tragit.
From travestire + -mento; Cognate with Piedmontese travestiment.
From Old French trufe, Old Occitan trufa. Compare tartufo for more.
From Latin ventūra (“the things that will come”, i.e. “the future”), neuter plural form of ventūrus (“which will come”), future active participle of veniō (“to come, approach”).
Borrowed from Classical Latin vīctus (“lifestyle; nourishment”), from vīvō (“to live; to survive”).
From a- + chiappare, from Vulgar Latin *clapāre, from Late Latin capulāre. Cognate with Sicilian acchiappari.
From Late Latin polygōnum, from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).
From French aérobie (coined in 1863 by Louis Pasteur, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”)) + -ico.
From Latin scandaculum. Cognate to French échantillon, Catalan escandall, Spanish escandallo.
From ferro (“iron”) + -are, or from a Late Latin ferrāre (cf. Classical Latin ferrātus), from Latin ferrum. Compare French ferrer, Catalan and Portuguese ferrar, Spanish herrar.
Borrowed from Latin taciturnus, from tacitus (“secret, tacit”).

Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “I am superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

From Latin axiōma, from Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma, “that which is thought to fit, a requisite, that which a pupil is required to know beforehand, a self-evident principle”), from ἀξιόω (axióō, “to think fit or worthy, require, demand”), from ἄξιος (áxios, “worthy, fit”, literally “weighing as much as, of like value”), from ἄγω (ágō, “to drive”).
Borrowed from English agnosticism. By surface analysis, agnostico (“agnostic”) + -ismo (“-ism”).
Borrowed from English fundamentalism. By surface analysis, fondamentale + -ismo.
From in- + forno + -are. Compare French enfourner; Catalan, Occitan, and Portuguese enfornar; Spanish enhornar; Friulian infornâ; Sardinian ifurrare.
From al- + lago (“lake”) + -are. Compare Sicilian allajari.
From Vulgar Latin argerem, from Latin aggerem (“rubble; mound; rampart”).
Borrowed from Latin aspīrātiōnem (“exhalation”). By surface analysis, aspira(re) (“to aspirate”, “to aspire”) + -zione (“-(a)tion”).
From Latin asperum (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese áspero (“rough”), French âpre, Romanian aspru.
Unadapted borrowing from English biogas. By surface analysis, bio- + gas.
Borrowed from Late Latin fortificātiōnem, from fortificō, from Latin fortis.
From turare (“to plug; to cork”) + -accio + -olo (noun suffixes).
Borrowed from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”).
From Latin bisōntem (“wild ox”), from Proto-Germanic *wisundaz (“wild ox, aurochs”).
From Late Latin blasphēmus, from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos).
From Vulgar Latin *mollīca, derived from Latin mollis (“soft”). Cognate with Sicilian muḍḍica.
From Greek βομβύλη (vomvýli). Compare Sicilian vùmmula.
Borrowed from Spanish vainilla, a diminutive form of vaina.
From tagliare (“to cut”) + -ino (noun-forming diminutive suffix). Doublet of tagliolino and tajarin.
From tagliata (“cut”, feminine past participle of tagliare) + -ella (diminutive suffix).
Borrowed from French casserole. Doublet of cassoeula.
From cerchio + -are, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *circlāre < Late Latin circulāre, from Latin circulārī, and therefore doublet of the borrowing circolare. Compare French cercler.
From Late Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew כְּרוּב (kərūḇ).
Borrowed from English cyclone. By surface analysis, ciclo + -one.
Borrowed from Latin clavicula. Compare the doublets cavicchia and caviglia.
From confeder(azione) (“confederation”) + -ale (“-al”), on the example of federale.
From congela(re) (“to freeze”) + -tore (“-er”, agent noun suffix).
From Late Latin contāgiōsus. By surface analysis, contagio (“contagion”) + -oso.
From cuscino + -etto (diminutive suffix). Cf. French coussinet.
From disastro + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese disastros.
Borrowed from Spanish doblón, augmentative of doble (“double”) (compare doppio).
Borrowed from Late Latin domātōrem, reshaping of Classical Latin domitōrem (“tamer”), derived from domō (“to tame”). By surface analysis, domare + -tore.
From earlier *dracone, from Latin dracōnem, accusative of dracō, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn). Compare drago, from the nominative.
From esente + -are. Cognate with Piedmontese esenté. Compare French exempter.
From Ancient Greek ἀσθένεια (asthéneia), from ἀσθενής (asthenḗs, “sick, weak”), from ἀ- (a-, “not, un-”) + σθένος (sthénos, “strength”).
Borrowed from Latin eunuchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
From figlio + -occio. Cognate with Sicilian figghiozzu.
Borrowed from French flacon. Doublet of fiasco.
From Occitan and Old Occitan flaut.
Borrowed from French forger. Doublet of fabbricare.
Borrowed from French forge, from Old French forge, from earlier faverge, from Latin fabrica, derived from faber (“forger, smith”). Doublet of fabbrica.

From forno + -ello (“diminutive suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Sicilian furneddu, Catalan fornell, Romansh furnel, Sardinian furredhu, Occitan fornèl, Portuguese fornilho, Spanish hornillo.
From metathesis of fracido, from Latin fracidus.
Borrowed from Latin fugitīvus and adapted to Italian fuggire.
Borrowed from Latin furentem, present participle of furō (“to rave, rage”).
From Latin iōcundus, alternative form of iūcundus.
Past participle of granire (“to granulate”), from grano (“grain”), from Latin granum (“grain”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm (“grain”).
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin grevem, alteration of Latin gravem. Doublet of grave.
From im- + pacchetto + -are. Compare Spanish and Catalan empaquetar, Portuguese empacotar.
From Latin lympha (“(clear) water”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē).
Borrowed from Spanish gallego and Portuguese galego, from Latin Gallaecus.
From Latin liquiritia, from Ancient Greek γλῠκύρριζα (glŭkúrrhiza), from γλῠκύς (glŭkús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”). Compare Sicilian rigulizzia.
From lottare + -tore, or from Latin luctātōrem.

From penzolo + -are or from Vulgar Latin *pendiolāre, from *pendiolus, from Latin pendulus, from pendō.
From piagnere + -ucolo + -are, from a variant of piangere. Doublet of piangiucchiare.
Borrowed from French manomètre. Ancient Greek μᾱ̆νός (mā̆nós) + -metro.
Either inherited or borrowed from Latin albūmen.
From pollo + -aio, or from Late Latin pullārium, from Latin pullārius (“pertaining to young animals or chicks”), from pullus (“young animal, chick”). Compare also pollario.
From porco + -eria. Compare Spanish porquería, Portuguese porcaria, Friulian porcarie, Venetan porcaria, Catalan porqueria, Romanian porcărie.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *porcīle. By surface analysis, porco (“pig”) + -ile (“place for keeping”).
From Latin prōlētārius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”) + -ato, from proles (“offspring, posterity”).
From Late Latin quintale, from Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār), ultimately from Latin centēnārium.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quotātiōnem.
From Latin duālis, derived from duō (“two”).

From Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum.
From Latin rabiōsus. By surface analysis, rabbia (“anger; rabies”) + -oso.
From Latin myrrha (also murra), from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), of Semitic origin.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin relictus, perfect passive participle of relinquō (“to abandon, relinquish”).
From Latin rectitūdinem (“straightness, uprightness”). By surface analysis, retto (“right, just”) + -itudine (“-itude”).
From Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología). By surface analysis, anto- (“related to flowers”) + -logia (“study of”).
From in- + cuneo + -are, or borrowed from in- + Latin cuneāre. Compare Sicilian ncugnari.
From Late Latin irradiāre, from in- + radiāre.
From Late Latin trapezium, from Ancient Greek τραπέζιον (trapézion).
Borrowed from French additionner, remodeled after native addizione.

From fossile + -izzare, on the model of French fossiliser.
From Latin natantem, present active participle of natō (“to swim”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos), from ὁμο- (homo-) + λόγος (lógos). By surface analysis, omo- + -logo.

Borrowed from Lombardic sterz (“handle of the plough”).
Calque of French remplacer, from ri- + impiazzare. Cognate to English reimplace, Catalan reemplaçar and Spanish reemplazar.
From Medieval Latin domnula, diminutive of domina. Compare Portuguese doninha.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk, used in manuscripts to mark passages”).
From Latin abstrūsus (“hidden, concealed”), the perfect passive participle of abstrūdō (“conceal, to push away”).
From codice (“code”) + -ficare, on the model of French codifier.
Borrowed from Latin exclamātiōnem. By surface analysis, esclamare + -zione. Likely a doublet of schiamazzo, if the latter was inherited from the Latin nominative exclamatio.
From Latin occultus, past participle form of occulō (“to hide, conceal”).

Borrowed from Latin antagonista, from Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”) (ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a combatant, pleader, actor”)), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “to antagonize”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin coenobīta.

Borrowed from Spanish sabana, from Taíno [Term?].
From Latin exa(u)gurātus, perfect passive participle of exaugurō (“to desecrate, make profane, exaugurate”), from ex- + augurō.
Either: * s- (“un-”) + con- + bussolo (“box”) + -are, literally “to separate what has been gathered (in a box)”. * s- (“un-”) + con- + bussola (“compass”) + -are.
From Latin mōbilia, neuter plural form of mōbilis (“movable”).

Borrowed from Late Latin masticātiōnem (“chewing”), derived from Latin masticō (“to chew”).

From Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”).

From Latin urtīca. Compare Sicilian ardìcula.

From Medieval Latin syringa, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, syrinx”).

From Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspīrātiōnem, from trānspīrō, from Latin trāns + spīrō.

From Latin strategema, from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).
From temere + -ibile. Compare Catalan and Spanish temible.

From Latin spīnōsus, or from spina + -oso.

Learned borrowing from Latin aureus. By surface analysis, aur- (“gold”, fossilized stem for oro) + -eo.
From Latin beātitūdinem (“happiness, blessedness, beatitude”), from beātus (“happy, blessed”).
Borrowed from French blocage, derived from bloquer (“to block”).

From cagione + -are or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *occāsionāre, from Latin occāsiāre. Cf. also accagionare, possibly from a root *accāsionāre. Compare Old French achoisoner, Romanian cășuna, cf. also Spanish ocasionar.

From Latin canistrum, from Ancient Greek κάναστρον (kánastron), κάνιστρον (kánistron). Compare English canister.
Borrowed from Spanish caníbal, from Taíno.

From cazzo + -eggiare. Compare with Sicilian cazzijari.

Borrowed from French démoraliser. By surface analysis, de- (“removal”) + morale (“moral”) + -izzare (“to make”).

From Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”). See also Old French dissenterie.
From dis- + umano; cognate with Piedmontese disuman.

From anacron(ismo) (“anachronism”) + -istico (“-istic”). By surface analysis, ana- (“reversal”) + cron(o-) (“time”) + -istico.

Internationalism. Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολυφωνία (poluphōnía). By surface analysis, poli- + -fonia.

Borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Medieval Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).
From Latin quintuplus. Equivalent to quinto + -uplo.

From Latin resīnōsus. By surface analysis, resina + -oso.
