From Latin psalterium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharyngem, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx).
From crivello + -are, from Late Latin cribellum, diminutive of Latin cribrum. Cf. also Late Latin cribellāre (“pass through a sieve; sift”).
From Late Latin cribellum, diminutive of Latin cribrum.
From Late Latin decasyllabus, from Ancient Greek δεκασύλλαβος (dekasúllabos), from δέκᾰ (dékă, “ten”) + σῠλλᾰβή (sŭllăbḗ, “syllable”). By surface analysis, deca- + sillabo.
From Latin similitūdinem (“likeness, similitude; simile”). By surface analysis, simile + -itudine.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós), from σῠ́ντᾰξῐς (sŭ́ntăxĭs, “syntax”) (compare sintassi).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin subtractiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin speculātīvus, from Latin speculor.
From Latin casula, a diminutive of casa.

From di- + ramo, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Romanian dărâma, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.
Borrowed from French blinder (“to reinforce”), derived from blinde (“piece of wood used as cover or protection”).
From Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.
Inherited from Latin flaccus. Compare French flache, Portuguese fraco, Sicilian fraccu and Spanish flaco.

Borrowed from Latin fluctus. Compare the inherited doublet fiotto.
From Latin fragor. Compare Spanish fragor.
Derived from Latin ēvolūtus (perfect passive participle of ēvolvō) + -ivo.
From Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) (combining form of αὐτός (autós)) + κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”) + -ης (-ēs).
Calque of English externality. First attested in 1987.
Borrowed from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).
From Latin subsidiārius. Compare with Friulian sussidiari.
From svalutare + -zione; cognate with Piedmontese svalutassion.
Probably a borrowing from French jeton.
Borrowed from French javelot, from Vulgar Latin *gabalottus (“spear”), derived from Gaulish *gabalos.
Borrowed from French gilet, itself from Italian giulecco.
From New Latin anthēra, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρά (anthērá), feminine form of ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”) from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower, blossom”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incīsīvus.

Borrowed from Latin Aethiopem, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin involūtus. Doublet of involto, which was inherited.

From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea-monster”)). The anatomy sense is so named from its resemblance to the seahorse. By surface analysis, hippo- + campus.
Unadapted borrowing from French dépliant (“leaflet, flyer”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lavativus, derived from Latin lavō (“to wash”). Compare French lavatif.
Borrowed from Late Latin peltātus, derived from Latin pelta (a kind of shield).
Borrowed from Latin longitūdinem (“length, longitude”), from longus (“long”).
From ri- + piegare, cf. also Latin replicō, replicāre.

Probably borrowed from Latin tēgula as a semi-learned term, or simply evolved from the word while the doublet teglia developed from another variant without the 'u'. Compare French tuile, Portuguese telha and Spanish teja.
From Latin trānsgressiōnem, derived from trānsgressus, perfect passive participle of trānsgredior (“to go over”).

From Medieval Latin marchionissa, feminine form of marchion, from Late Latin marcha, from Frankish *markōn (“to mark, mark out, to press with the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“area, region, edge, rim, border”). Cognate with Sicilian marchisa.
From a- + buffare (“to blow; to huff”) + -are + -si.
Borrowed from English shaman, from German Schamane, from Russian шама́н (šamán), from Evenki шама̄н (şamān), сама̄н (samān).
From Latin somnolentus, derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From Late Latin nārīcem, ultimately derived from Latin nāris.
From pagare + -abile; cognate with Piedmontese pagàbil.
From French lamantin, alteration of Spanish manatí.
Borrowed from English cybernetics, from Ancient Greek κυβερνητική (kubernētikḗ).
From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).
Borrowed from English agnostic, derived from Ancient Greek ἄγνωστος (ágnōstos). By surface analysis, a- (“un-”, negative prefix) + gnostico (“gnostic”).
From New Latin glottidem, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).

From Late Latin epiglottidem, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγλωττίς (epiglōttís) derived from γλῶττα (glôtta), variant of γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). By surface analysis, epi- (“above”, “over”) + glottide (“glottis”).
From Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos), from οἰσέμεν (oisémen), future form of φέρω (phérō, “I carry”) + ἔφαγον (éphagon, “I ate”).
From Ancient Greek μᾰρασμός (mărasmós, “withering”), from μᾰραίνω (măraínō, “to waste, wither”).
From biometria + -ico. By surface analysis, bio- + -metrico.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dīgestīvus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin formativus.
From Late Latin molīnārius, from molīnus, from Latin molō. Doublet of mulinaro, molinaro, and mulinaio, from regional variants. Compare French meunier.
From Latin amātōrem. Doublet of amateur.
From Latin apud with the confluence of ad post.
Borrowed from Latin gentīlicius. By surface analysis, gentile (in the historical sense “relating to a gens”) + -izio.
From Latin gentiana, possibly ultimately from Illyrian [Term?].
Borrowed from Late Latin contrādictōrius (“contradictory”), from Latin contrādīcō (“to speak against; contradict”).
Borrowed from Old French corocier, corucier, from Vulgar Latin *corruptiāre, from Latin corruptus, perfect passive participle of corrumpō (“to corrupt”). Doublet of crucciare.
Borrowed from Latin dēlinquere (“to fail in one's duty”), from de- + linquō (“to neglect”), present infinitive form of linquō (“to leave”).
Borrowed from Latin convexus, and adapted to Italian.
From Latin dēsuētus (“unused”), from dēsuēscō (“to disuse”).
From *fiorello + -ino (diminutive suffix), from fiore + -ello (diminutive suffix). Compare Sicilian ciuriḍḍuzzu.
From Ancient Greek ἐμφατικός (emphatikós), variant of ἐμφαντικός (emphantikós), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “I show, present”).
Borrowed from French minoritaire, from minorité. By surface analysis, minorità + -ario.
From Late Latin furnārius, from Latin furnus (“oven”). By surface analysis, forno + -aio.
Inherited from Late Latin ganathus, from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos).
Formed from percetto + -ivo (from Latin perceptus), based on French perceptif, or borrowed from Medieval Latin perceptivus.
Borrowed from Late Latin incrēdulitātem, from Latin incrēdulus.
Borrowed from Latin inūtilitātem (“uselessness”), derived from inūtilis (“useless”).
Calque of French similaire, from Latin simile + -are. Compare also Medieval Latin similāris.
Borrowed from French linguiste, from Latin lingua + -iste.
Borrowed from French légaliser. By surface analysis, legale (“legal”) + -izzare (“to make”).
From paglia + -aio, or from Latin paleārium.
Borrowed from Latin prĕcārius. See also preghiera.
From Latin Athenaeum, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓θήναιον (Ăthḗnaion).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσυμμετρίᾱ (asummetríā). By surface analysis, a- + simmetria.
Inherited from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion).
Borrowed from Latin angelicus, from angelus (“angel”). By surface analysis, angelo + -ico.
From Latin amphitheātrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron). By surface analysis, anfi- + teatro.
Inherited from Late Latin appārēscente (“beginning to appear”, singular ablative present participle of appārēscō (“to begin to appear”), inchoative of Latin appāreō (“to appear”)).
Borrowed from Spanish achaque, from Arabic شَكَا (šakā, “to complain”).
From muscolo + -oso, or from Latin musculōsus.
From Latin alpēstris. By surface analysis, Alpi + -estre.
From French pachyderme, from Ancient Greek παχύδερμος (pakhúdermos), from παχύς (pakhús, “thick”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).
From a- (“to”) + guant(o) (“glove”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From a- (“towards”) + moglie (“wife”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

From Latin lūcus (“grove sacred to a deity”), from Old Latin loucos, from Proto-Indo-European *lowkós (“open space, clearing”), derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include English lea (“meadow”), Hindi लोक (lok, “public” ← “world”), Lithuanian laũkas (“field”).
From ri- (“re-”) + mescolare (“to mix, stir, blend, shuffle”).
Borrowed from Latin althaea, from Ancient Greek ἀλθαία (althaía, “marshmallow, Althaea officinalis”), from ἀλθαίνω (althaínō, “to heal”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mendācem (“mendacious, lying, false”).
From rin- + culo + -are, calque of French reculer.
Learned borrowing from Latin scrība. Doublet of scrivano.
From giallo (“yellow”) + rosso (“red”), the colors of the flag of Rome and of the shirts of the Roma football/soccer team.
From Medieval Latin stigmatizō, from Medieval Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō). By surface analysis, stigma + -izzare.
From Latin suppositiōnem, from sub- (“under”) + positiō (“position; theme”).
Borrowed from Latin vorācitātem. Cognates include Catalan voracitat, French voracité and Spanish voracidad.
From in- + farina (“flour”) + -are. Compare Catalan enfarinar, French enfariner, Portuguese enfarinhar, Romanian înfăina, Sicilian nfarinari, Spanish enharinar.
From Latin apotheōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis).
From French guinder (“to raise, hoist”, figurative “to emphasize”).
From Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).
Borrowed from Late Latin acēdia. Doublet of acedia.

From Latin angustus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰ-. The correspondence of Latin short /u/ to Italian /u/ (rather than Italian /o/ as in agosto, mosto) indicates that the form is possibly a semi-learned borrowing (compare gusto).
From Spanish bauprés, from French beaupré, from Dutch boegspriet.
From a- (“to, towards”) + quieto (“quiet, peaceful”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
From French cambuse, from Middle Dutch kabuys.
Borrowed from French caréner. By surface analysis, carena (“keel”) + -are.
From Latin āmanuēnsis. By surface analysis, a + mano + -ense.
Borrowed from Spanish hamaca (“hammock, swing”), from Taíno.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).
From Latin apostasia, from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “defection, revolt”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin forāneus, from Latin foris. First attested 17th century.
From vendemmia (“grape harvest”) + -aio, calque of French vendémiaire.
From bruma (“mist, haze”) + -aio, calque of French brumaire.
From Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion).
From Old Occitan beltat, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem, derived from Latin bellus (“beautiful”).
From bottega + -aio. See also Latin apothecārius. Cognate with Sicilian putigaru.
From Latin bulla (“seal”) + -etta (diminutive suffix), from the resemblance.
From borro (“ditch”) + -one, the stem probably a northern form of botro.
Borrowed from Spanish marrano, from Arabic مُحَرَّم (muḥarram, “forbidden”).
From Latin nāvigium (with a change of suffix), or through a Late Vulgar Latin form *nāvilium (compare French navire (Old French navilie), Old Occitan navili). Doublet of navigio.
From Latin cālīgō, cālīginem (“fog”), of uncertain origin. Compare Portuguese caligem (“fog”) and Spanish calina (“haze”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cālīginōsus (“foggy, misty; dark”).

From Vulgar Latin *prōda, from Latin prōra (via dissimilation), borrowed from Ancient Greek πρῷρα (prōîra), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-, form of *por-. Doublet of prua and prora. Compare Spanish proa.
Borrowed from French propulsif, from Latin prōpulsus.
Borrowed from French rouler. Doublet of rotolare.
Borrowed from Latin Carthāginem, from Phoenician 𐤒𐤓𐤕-𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤕 (qrt-ḥdšt, “New City”).
From svantaggio + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese svantagios.
Borrowed from French calorique. By surface analysis, calori- + -ico.
From antropometria + -ico. By surface analysis, antropo- + -metrico.
From Ancient Greek ἄπολις (ápolis, “without city, state or country”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).
From Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos, “catarrh, head cold”).
From Latin catasta, from Ancient Greek κατάστασις (katástasis, “establishment, institution, method, condition”).
Borrowed from French caoutchouc, from Quechua kawchu.
Borrowed from Late Latin causālis, derived from Latin causa. By surface analysis, causa (“cause”) + -ale (“-al”, “pertaining to”).
Derived from Late Latin clāmorōsus. By surface analysis, clamore + -oso.
From 16ᵗʰ-century Spanish xícara (modern jícara), from Classical Nahuatl xīcalli.
Borrowed from Latin contumāx (“stubborn, obstinate”). Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese contumaz, English contumacious.
From Late Latin claustellum (“keyhole”), diminutive of Latin claustrum. Influenced by Italian chiave (“key”).
From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”). By surface analysis, fiducia + -ario.
From Occitan chiminièra, from Old French cheminee.
Perhaps from vulgar forms like *sorcipiglio, *sorpiciglio, from Latin supercilium (“frown”). Compare sopracciglio (“eyebrow”).
Calque of French informatiser, from informatica + -izzare.
Borrowed from Latin inimīcitia, from inimīcus.
Borrowed from Latin collūctātiōnem. By surface analysis, colluttare (“to fight, scuffle”) + -zione.
From Latin mittentem, present active participle of mittō.
Borrowed from Latin pecūlātus, from Latin pecūlor (“to embezzle”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin persecūtōrem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin postilla, from post illa (verba) "after those words".
Borrowed from Latin quaesitus. Doublet of chiesto.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin rendita, from the past participle of Late Latin rendō (“to give back, yield”).
From Late Latin ārsūra, from Latin ārsus.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσφυξία (asphuxía, “stopping of the pulse”).
Borrowed from Latin augustus. Doublet of the inherited agosto.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θρόμβωσις (thrómbōsis, “curdling”), derived from θρόμβος (thrómbos, “clot, curd”).
From Latin benna (“carriage”), from Gaulish benna (“carriage”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bitūminōsus. By surface analysis, bitume + -oso.
From Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus.
Borrowed from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus.
Inherited from Latin natāre (“swim, float”). Doublet of nuotare.
From the intermediate Vulgar Latin *ri(ji)one(m), from the masculinization of Latin regiōnem. Compare the borrowed doublet regione. Cognate with Sicilian rijuni.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin compūnctiōnem.
Blend of mieti(trice) (“harvesting machine”) + trebbiatrice (“threshing machine”). By surface analysis, mietere (“to harvest”) + trebbiare (“to thresh”) + -trice (female agent noun suffix).
Calque of French mouvementer, from movimento + -are.
From Latin concussiōnem (“shaking”, noun), derived from concutiō (“to shake violently”).
From Latin concupiscentia, from concupīscō (“to desire strongly, to desire eagerly; to covet”).
Borrowed from Old French oreillier, from oreille (“ear”). By surface analysis, orecchia + -are.
Borrowed from Old French ostel, from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospitale.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus.
From proseguire + -mento; cognate with Piedmontese proseguiment.
Learned borrowing from Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-. Doublet of oro.
Of Southern Italian origin, from Latin sapientem (“discerning, wise”), present active participle of sapiō (“to be wise”). Doublet of sapiente.
Borrowed from Latin silvestrem. Cf. salvastrella.
From coriandro + -olo, with loss of the second /r/.
Borrowed from Latin correctivus, from correctus.
From Latin corruptōrem, from corruptus, past participle of corrumpō, corrumpere (compare corrompere).
Learned borrowing from Latin trepidātiōnem (“agitation, trepidation”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis. Doublet of triste, a borrowing from Latin.
From tutto (“everything”) + fare (“to do”), calque of French (bonne à) tout faire.
Borrowed from Latin vitiōsus. Doublet of vezzoso.
From Latin cultōrem, derived from colō (“to cultivate; to inhabit; to worship”).
Borrowed from French décalquer. First attested in 1758.
From settanta + -enario. Cognate with French septantenaire.
Borrowed from Late Latin ficticius, from Latin fictus.
From centimetro + -are. Literally, “[to divide] into centimeters”.
From a- + casa (“house”) + -are. Compare also Spanish casar (“to marry”), Romanian căsători.
Borrowed from Latin acquiēscentem (“resting, acquiescing”), present active participle of acquiēscō (“to rest; to acquiesce”).
Borrowed from Latin tunica. Compare the inherited tonaca.
From aero- + -statico, on the model of French aérostatique.
Inherited from Latin adēscāre (“to feed, fatten”), from ad + ēsca (“food”).
From Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
Borrowed from French autodidacte, from Ancient Greek αὐτοδίδακτος (autodídaktos), derived from αὐτός (autós, “self”) + the root of διδάσκω (didáskō, “I teach”).
From Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”).
From Late Latin delavāre, from Latin de + lavāre.
From a- (“to, towards”) + mare (“sea”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
Borrowed from Latin andrōnem from Ancient Greek ἀνδρών (andrṓn).
From Latin anthrōpophagus, from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποφάγος (anthrōpophágos).
From diritto + -tura or from Latin dīrēctūra.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin exsistentiālis.
From arma (“weapon”) + -aiolo (suffix indicating a profession or activity).
From a- + riccio + -are. Compare Spanish rizar, Portuguese riçar and French hérisser.
Borrowed from Latin aspidem, from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield; Egyptian cobra”). Doublet of aspe.
From assillo (“horsefly, gadfly; nagging worry”) + -are. Compare Sicilian siḍḍijari (often incorrectly written as siḍḍiari).
From a- + sottile (“thin”) + -are, or from a- + sottigliare (now obsolete), from Late Latin subtiliāre, from Latin subtīlis.
From astro- + -nautica, on the model of aeronautica.
From Ancient Greek ἄτονος (átonos), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + τόνος (tónos, “tension, tone”).
Borrowed from Latin aurifer. By surface analysis, auri- + -ifero.
Borrowed from French autocratie, from Medieval Greek αὐτοκρατία (autokratía).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin dēsertiōnem, from Latin dēsertus.
From dis- + inserire. First attested in 1940.
From dispetto + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese dispetos.
Borrowed from Old French bai, or Old Occitan, ultimately from Latin badius.
Via Latin balaustum, balaustium, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin anguem, form of anguis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éngʷʰis (“snake”).
From battere (“to beat”) + -tore (“-er”, agent noun suffix).
From bevone, from Late Latin bibōnem, from Latin bibō, bibere + -ō, -ōnem. By surface analysis, bere + -one.
From bi- + camera + -ale, a calque of English bicameral.
Inherited from Late Latin drappus, probably of Germanic or possibly Celtic origin.
Deverbal from bilicare (“to balance”) + -o, itself inherited from Vulgar Latin *umbilicāre, derived from Latin umbilicus.
Inherited from Late Latin bisaccium, bi- + sacca. Compare dialectal English bysack.
From bi- (“bi-, two”) + Latin secāre (“to cut”). First attested in 1905.
Borrowed from Latin diūturnus (“long-lasting”), derived from diū (“continually, all day”).
From Latin Rudolphus, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþiwulfaz (literally “glorious wolf”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bonificāre. By surface analysis, buono + -ficare.
From Latin Zacharias, from Koine Greek, from Hebrew.
Borrowed from Late Latin duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō.
From Medieval Latin Bulgarus (“Bulgarian; swindler, usurer”) + -are.
From cane (“dog”) + -esco, using the root found in cagna (“female dog”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calidizāre. Derivable from caldo + -eggiare.
Borrowed from French calotte. Compare Portuguese calota.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “I explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “I lead, guide”).
From Latin mūnificentia, derived from mūnificēns (“bountiful”).
From Latin ēbrius, from Proto-Italic *ēɣʷrios, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ēgʷʰryos, derived from the root *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”).
From Ancient Greek τρίπτυχος (tríptukhos, “consisting of three layers, threefold”), from τρι- (tri-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “a fold”).
From Latin petrōsus or from pietra + -oso. Doublet of petroso.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin exemplificāre, from Latin exemplum (“example”).
Borrowed from French hématie, from Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin imperscrūtābilis.
From Latin efferātus, from efferō (“to brutalize”), from ferus (“wild”), related to Italian fiero.
Learned borrowing from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek σωματικός (sōmatikós, “bodily”), from σῶμα (sôma, “body”). By surface analysis, soma + -atico.
From Late Latin caprifolium, from Latin caper + folium.
Inherited from Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna. By surface analysis, farina + -oso.

From Latin epigonī, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγονοι (epígonoi), plural form of ἐπίγονος (epígonos, “offspring, descendant”), from ἐπιγίγνομαι (epigígnomai, “to come after”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”), from γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to become”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin hermeticus.
From Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archia (“rule”, “government”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retorsiōnem, derived from retorsus, alternative form of Latin retortus, perfect passive participle of retorqueō.
Borrowed from Late Latin exūberantia, derived from Latin exūberāns, present active participle of exūberō (“to abound or flourish”).
From Latin salix, from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥H-ik- (“willow”). Doublet of Salgari.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin temporizāre, from Latin tempus (“time”); adapted to the suffix -eggiare.
Inherited from Late Latin variola f, with a change in gender.

Uncertain. Most sources originate it from Late Latin faluppa (“chaff, waste”) (from which also the doublet faloppa), influenced from/crossed with a derivate of Latin volvere. Other sources theorizes a sole derivation from volvere. Lastly, it may be related to/based on Old French (en)velopper, which either derives from one of the previously mentioned roots or, through an unattested Vulgar Latin term, from Germanic (compare with the (unsourced) theories displayed for the english terms envelop, develop).
Inherited from Latin numerus (via old intermediary forms *nomero > *nombero > *nobero), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”). Doublet of numero, a borrowing.
(Possibly borrowed) from Latin opācus (“shaded, shady, dark”), itself of unknown origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *farrum, from Latin far (“emmer”).
From fiacc(o) (“exhaust, weary”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix). Compare Sicilian ciaccari.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin novilūnium.
Borrowed from Latin frātricīda. By surface analysis, fratri- (“brother”, fossilized stem of fratello) + -cida.
From Late Latin trepanum, from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, borer”).
From the variant formicola of formica (“ant”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation suffix). Cf. also French fourmiller.
Borrowed from French frange, from Late Latin fimbria, from Latin fimbriae. Compare Sicilian frinza.
Borrowed from French jade, from Spanish piedra de ijada (“loin stone”), because of its purported property of curing kindney stones.
From lavare + -tura, or from a Vulgar Latin *lavatūra, from Latin lavō. Compare French lavure, Sicilian lavatura, Spanish lavadura, Romanian lături.
Borrowed from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin. Doublet of the inherited aragosta.
Learned borrowing from Latin ostentātiōnem (“exhibition, showing off”).
From Latin portentum, participle of portendere, from portendō (“to predict, to foretell”).
Borrowed from Latin Cȳrēnaeus, from Ancient Greek Κυρηναῖος (Kurēnaîos), from Κυρήνη (Kurḗnē) + -αῖος (-aîos).
From corniolo, ultimately from Latin cornus.
From discernere + -mento; cognate with Piedmontese disserniment.
Borrowed from Spanish fanfarrón, from Arabic فَرْفَار (farfār), perhaps via French fanfaron.
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin fulgor, fulgōrem (“lightning; flash”).
From Old French garant, probably from Frankish *werênd, *warjan, akin to German gewähren (“to grant”) and Old High German wërênt.
Borrowed from Old French joir. Doublet of godere.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impostūra.
Borrowed from Latin ineffābilis (“unutterable, unpronounceable”), derived from effābilis (“utterable”), derived from effor (“to speak, say out, utter”), derived from for (“to speak, talk, say”).
From Late Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; phlegm”).
Borrowed from Spanish flojo, from Latin fluxus. Doublet of frocio. Compare Sicilian froscia.
Inherited from Latin lībātiōnem. Compare libazione, a borrowing from Latin.
From Latin licentiōsus, from licentia (“license, freedom”).
From mentire + -tore, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *mentitōrem, from Latin mentior. Compare French menteur, Romanian mințitor.
Borrowed from Late Latin parasceue, from Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ, “preparazione”).
From Latin perniciōsus. By surface analysis, pernicie (“disaster”, “ruin”) + -oso (“-ous”, suffix denoting presence of an attribute).
Inherited from Latin pēnsiōnem. Doublet of pensione, which was borrowed.
From Latin prīscus, from earlier *priuscus, derived from prior (“former”, “previous”), from Proto-Italic *priōs, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per (“to go over”).
Borrowed from Late Latin prōclāmātiōnem, from Latin prōclāmō.
Learned borrowing from Classical Latin pulcher, pulchrum.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin sūdārium, from Latin sūdor.
